Again, away from points where cancellation is invalid, this reduces to
x\,dx=z\,dz.
Integrating gives
x^2-z^2=C_2.
Therefore, the flow line through (x_0,y_0,z_0) is described implicitly by
x^2-y^2=x_0^2-y_0^2,\qquad
x^2-z^2=x_0^2-z_0^2.
These two equations describe the curve as the intersection of two surfaces. This is common in three-dimensional field-line problems. A parametrization is not always necessary unless the question explicitly asks for one.

Some plane vector fields are easier to describe in polar coordinates. In polar coordinates, a point is described by a distance r\ge 0 from the origin and an angle \theta. The corresponding unit vectors are
\hat{\mathbf r}=\cos\theta\,\mathbf i+\sin\theta\,\mathbf j,
and
\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}=-\sin\theta\,\mathbf i+\cos\theta\,\mathbf j.
The vector \hat{\mathbf r} points radially outward, in the direction of increasing r. The vector \hat{\boldsymbol\theta} points tangentially, in the direction of increasing \theta. These unit vectors depend on \theta, so they change from point to point. They are not fixed like \mathbf i and \mathbf j. They are also not defined at the origin, because the angle \theta is not defined there.
A plane vector field can be written in polar form as
\mathbf F(r,\theta)=F_r(r,\theta)\hat{\mathbf r}+F_\theta(r,\theta)\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}.
Here F_r(r,\theta) is the radial component and F_\theta(r,\theta) is the tangential component. The subscripts r and \theta label polar components. They do not mean partial derivatives.
To find field lines in polar form, suppose the curve is described by
r=r(\theta).
The position vector is
\mathbf r=r\hat{\mathbf r}.
A small displacement along the curve is
d\mathbf r=dr\,\hat{\mathbf r}+r\,d\theta\,\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}.
The first term is radial displacement. The second term is tangential displacement. The factor r appears because a small change d\theta sweeps out an arc length r\,d\theta. For the curve to be a field line, this displacement must be parallel to
F_r(r,\theta)\hat{\mathbf r}+F_\theta(r,\theta)\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}.
Therefore,
\frac{dr}{F_r(r,\theta)}=\frac{r\,d\theta}{F_\theta(r,\theta)}.
When F_\theta(r,\theta)\ne 0, this can be written as
\frac{dr}{d\theta}=r\frac{F_r(r,\theta)}{F_\theta(r,\theta)}.
This is the polar-coordinate field-line equation. It should be used only after the polar components have been correctly identified. A purely radial field, where F_\theta=0, has field lines with constant \theta. A purely tangential field, where F_r=0, has field lines with constant r.
For example, consider
\mathbf F=\hat{\mathbf r}+\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}.
Here
F_r=1,\qquad F_\theta=1.
The polar field-line equation becomes
\frac{dr}{1}=\frac{r\,d\theta}{1},
so
\frac{dr}{d\theta}=r.
Solving gives
r=Ce^\theta,
where C>0 is a constant. Thus the field lines are logarithmic spirals. This makes sense geometrically: the field has both an outward radial component and a tangential component, so a particle following the field both moves outward and turns.
As a second polar example, consider
\mathbf F=r\hat{\mathbf r}-\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}.
Here
F_r=r,\qquad F_\theta=-1.
The polar field-line equation gives
\frac{dr}{r}=\frac{r\,d\theta}{-1}.
Equivalently,
\frac{dr}{d\theta}=-r^2.
Separating variables gives
\frac{dr}{r^2}=-d\theta.
Integrating gives
-\frac{1}{r}=-\theta+C,
or
\frac{1}{r}=\theta+C_1.
Therefore,
r=\frac{1}{\theta+C_1}.
This example shows why one should not guess that every polar field line is a circle or an exponential spiral. The equation depends on the ratio between the radial component and the tangential component.
The gradient gives an important bridge between scalar fields and vector fields. If f(x,y,z) is a scalar field, then its gradient is
\nabla f=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\mathbf i+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\mathbf j+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\mathbf k.
This is a vector field because it assigns a vector to each point where the partial derivatives exist. The gradient points in the direction of fastest increase of the scalar field and is perpendicular to the level surfaces of the scalar field. Thus a scalar field can produce a vector field by differentiation.
Not every vector field arises as the gradient of a scalar field. The special vector fields that do arise in this way are studied separately as conservative fields. For the present section, the essential distinction is simpler: a scalar field assigns one number to each point, while a vector field assigns a vector to each point. Field lines are curves tangent to those assigned vectors. In Cartesian coordinates, the basis vectors \mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k are fixed; in polar coordinates, \hat{\mathbf r} and \hat{\boldsymbol\theta} move from point to point. Most mistakes in this section come from confusing these roles: mistaking a component for a derivative, treating a vector field as a single vector, forgetting zero-field points, or applying the field-line formulas where a denominator vanishes.
The section’s main idea is therefore that fields describe spatially varying quantities. Scalar fields describe quantities with size only; vector fields describe quantities with size and direction. Field lines then convert a vector field into a family of curves that make the direction of the field visible and computable.

math-2/notes/16-2-conservative-fields-17.title: 16.2 Conservative Fields
math-2/notes/16-2-conservative-fields-17.content:
16.2 Conservative Fields
A vector field assigns a vector to each point of a domain. In physical language, the vector may describe a force, an electric field, or a velocity. In mathematical language, it is a function whose output is a vector rather than a scalar. The central question in this section is whether such a vector field can be described more economically by a single scalar function. Instead of storing a full vector at every point, can we store one number at every point and recover the vector field by differentiating that number in space?
This question appears naturally after the gradient. The gradient turns a scalar field into a vector field. If \varphi(x,y,z) is a scalar function, then its gradient is
\nabla \varphi(x,y,z)
=
\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x}\mathbf{i}
+
\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial y}\mathbf{j}
+
\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial z}\mathbf{k}.
Here \varphi assigns one real number to each point, while \nabla\varphi assigns a vector to each point. The vector \nabla\varphi points in the direction in which \varphi increases fastest, and its length gives the maximum rate of increase. Conservative fields ask the reverse question: given a vector field \mathbf{F}, can we find a scalar field \varphi such that \mathbf{F} is exactly the gradient of \varphi?
A vector field \mathbf{F} on a domain D is called conservative if there exists a scalar function \varphi:D\to\mathbb{R} such that
\mathbf{F}=\nabla \varphi
\quad \text{on } D.
The function \varphi is called a scalar potential, or simply a potential, for the vector field. In three dimensions, if
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)
=
F_1(x,y,z)\mathbf{i}
+
F_2(x,y,z)\mathbf{j}
+
F_3(x,y,z)\mathbf{k},
then the equation \mathbf{F}=\nabla\varphi means
F_1=\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x},
\qquad
F_2=\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial y},
\qquad
F_3=\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial z}.
This is a strong requirement. A general vector field has several component functions, and those components may vary independently. A conservative field is special because all its components come from differentiating one underlying scalar function.
The potential is not unique. If \varphi is a potential for \mathbf{F}, then \varphi+C is also a potential for every constant C, because
\nabla(\varphi+C)=\nabla\varphi.
This is the multivariable version of the fact that an antiderivative in one-variable calculus is determined only up to an additive constant. If the domain has several disconnected pieces, the additive constant may even be chosen separately on each connected component, because there is no path inside the domain connecting those pieces.
A useful physical convention must be separated from the mathematical definition. In this section, a conservative field is usually written as
\mathbf{F}=\nabla\varphi.
In many physics problems, especially force-field problems, the force is instead written as
\mathbf{F}=-\nabla U,
where U is potential energy. The minus sign means that the force points in the direction in which potential energy decreases fastest. For example, if a spring has potential energy
U(x)=\frac12kx^2,
then
F(x)=-\frac{dU}{dx}=-kx.
The force points back toward x=0, where the potential energy is smaller. The difference between \mathbf{F}=\nabla\varphi and \mathbf{F}=-\nabla U is only a sign convention: if a force satisfies \mathbf{F}=-\nabla U, then it also satisfies \mathbf{F}=\nabla\varphi with \varphi=-U. In exam problems, the sign in the question matters. If the question asks for U such that \mathbf{F}=-\nabla U, then the components of -\mathbf{F}, not \mathbf{F}, must be integrated to find U.
The simplest conservative fields are obtained directly by differentiating a given potential. For example, let
\varphi(x,y,z)
=
\left(
\frac{x^2}{a^2}
+
\frac{y^2}{b^2}
+
\frac{z^2}{c^2}
\right)^{1/2},
\qquad a,b,c>0.
Define
S(x,y,z)=
\frac{x^2}{a^2}
+
\frac{y^2}{b^2}
+
\frac{z^2}{c^2}.
Then \varphi=S^{1/2}. By the chain rule,
\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x}
=
\frac12S^{-1/2}\frac{2x}{a^2}
=
\frac{x}{a^2\sqrt{S}}.
Similarly,
\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial y}
=
\frac{y}{b^2\sqrt{S}},
\qquad
\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial z}
=
\frac{z}{c^2\sqrt{S}}.
Therefore the conservative field generated by this potential is
\nabla\varphi
=
\frac{x}{a^2\sqrt{S}}\mathbf{i}
+
\frac{y}{b^2\sqrt{S}}\mathbf{j}
+
\frac{z}{c^2\sqrt{S}}\mathbf{k}.
This direction, from potential to field, is mechanically straightforward: compute the gradient. The harder direction is the reverse direction: given a vector field, decide whether a potential exists and then find it.
To understand the test for conservativeness, begin in two dimensions. Suppose
\mathbf{F}(x,y)=F_1(x,y)\mathbf{i}+F_2(x,y)\mathbf{j}
is conservative, so \mathbf{F}=\nabla\varphi. Then
F_1=\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x},
\qquad
F_2=\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial y}.
If the relevant second partial derivatives are continuous, then mixed partial derivatives of \varphi are equal:
\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial y\,\partial x}
=
\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial y}.
Therefore,
\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial y}
=
\frac{\partial F_2}{\partial x}.
This is a necessary condition for a plane vector field to be conservative. It says that the way the first component changes in the y-direction must agree with the way the second component changes in the x-direction.
In three dimensions, if
\mathbf{F}
=
F_1\mathbf{i}+F_2\mathbf{j}+F_3\mathbf{k}
is conservative, then the corresponding necessary conditions are
\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial y}
=
\frac{\partial F_2}{\partial x},
\qquad
\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial z}
=
\frac{\partial F_3}{\partial x},
\qquad
\frac{\partial F_2}{\partial z}
=
\frac{\partial F_3}{\partial y}.
These equations say that the cross-partial derivatives of the vector-field components must match. The same condition can be expressed by saying that the Jacobian matrix D\mathbf{F} is symmetric. The Jacobian matrix of a vector field is the matrix containing all first partial derivatives of its component functions:
D\mathbf{F}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial y} & \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial z} \\
\dfrac{\partial F_2}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial F_2}{\partial y} & \dfrac{\partial F_2}{\partial z} \\
\dfrac{\partial F_3}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial F_3}{\partial y} & \dfrac{\partial F_3}{\partial z}
\end{pmatrix}.
A matrix is symmetric when entries mirrored across the main diagonal are equal. In this context, symmetry is exactly the system of equalities above.
The partial-derivative test must not be used without thinking about the domain. A domain is connected if any two points in it can be joined by a curve that stays inside the domain. A connected domain is simply connected if every closed curve in the domain can be continuously shrunk to a point without leaving the domain. Intuitively, a simply connected domain has no holes. On a simply connected domain, for a continuously differentiable vector field in two or three dimensions, the matching partial-derivative conditions are enough to conclude that the field is conservative. On a domain with a hole, the same derivative conditions may not be enough.
A basic nonconservative example is the rotational field
\mathbf{F}(x,y)=\omega(-y\mathbf{i}+x\mathbf{j}),
where \omega is a constant. Its components are
F_1(x,y)=-\omega y,
\qquad
F_2(x,y)=\omega x.
Then
\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial y}=-\omega,
\qquad
\frac{\partial F_2}{\partial x}=\omega.
These are equal only if \omega=0. Therefore a genuine rotational field, with \omega\neq0, is not conservative. Geometrically, this agrees with the picture: the field circulates around the origin rather than arising as the gradient of a scalar height function.
The domain warning is subtler. A hole in the domain does not automatically mean that a field is not conservative. It only means that the simple partial-derivative test is no longer sufficient by itself. Compare the two fields
\mathbf{F}(x,y)
=
\frac{x\mathbf{i}-y\mathbf{j}}{x^2+y^2},
\qquad (x,y)\neq(0,0),
and
\mathbf{G}(x,y)
=
\frac{x\mathbf{i}+y\mathbf{j}}{x^2+y^2},
\qquad (x,y)\neq(0,0).
Both are defined on the punctured plane \mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}, which has a hole at the origin.
For \mathbf{F},
F_1=\frac{x}{x^2+y^2},
\qquad
F_2=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}.
The cross-partials are
\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial y}
=
\frac{-2xy}{(x^2+y^2)^2},
and
\frac{\partial F_2}{\partial x}
=
\frac{2xy}{(x^2+y^2)^2}.
These are not equal in general, so \mathbf{F} is not conservative. This conclusion follows before any deeper domain discussion is needed.
For \mathbf{G},
G_1=\frac{x}{x^2+y^2},
\qquad
G_2=\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}.
This field is conservative, even though the domain has a hole, because it has the explicit potential
\varphi(x,y)
=
\frac12\ln(x^2+y^2).
Indeed,
\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x}
=
\frac12\cdot\frac{2x}{x^2+y^2}
=
\frac{x}{x^2+y^2},
and
\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial y}
=
\frac12\cdot\frac{2y}{x^2+y^2}
=
\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}.
Thus \nabla\varphi=\mathbf{G}. This example prevents a common mistake: a non-simply connected domain does not automatically destroy conservativeness. It only prevents the cross-partial test from being a complete guarantee.
The standard example of a field that passes the cross-partial test locally but still fails to have a global potential on the punctured plane is
\mathbf{H}(x,y)
=
\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}\mathbf{i}
+
\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\mathbf{j},
\qquad (x,y)\neq(0,0).
This field satisfies
\frac{\partial H_1}{\partial y}
=
\frac{\partial H_2}{\partial x}
on its domain, but it has no single-valued potential on the whole punctured plane. Locally it behaves like the gradient of the polar angle \theta, but \theta cannot be chosen continuously as one single-valued function all the way around the origin. After one full turn, the angle has changed by 2\pi. The hole prevents a global potential from existing.
Once a field passes the appropriate conservative-field test, the potential is found by integrating one component at a time. The crucial point is that when integrating with respect to one variable, the “constant” of integration may depend on the other variables.
For example, consider
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)
=
(2xy-z^2)\mathbf{i}
+
(2yz+x^2)\mathbf{j}
-
(2zx-y^2)\mathbf{k}.
First check the compatibility conditions. The components are
F_1=2xy-z^2,
\qquad
F_2=2yz+x^2,
\qquad
F_3=-(2zx-y^2)=-2zx+y^2.
Now
\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial y}=2x
=
\frac{\partial F_2}{\partial x},
\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial z}=-2z
=
\frac{\partial F_3}{\partial x},
and
\frac{\partial F_2}{\partial z}=2y
=
\frac{\partial F_3}{\partial y}.
The field is defined on all of \mathbb{R}^3, which is simply connected, so these equalities show that the field is conservative.
To find \varphi, start from
\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x}=2xy-z^2.
Integrating with respect to x gives
\varphi(x,y,z)=x^2y-xz^2+C_1(y,z).
The term C_1(y,z) may depend on y and z, because it disappears when differentiating with respect to x. Now use the second component:
\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial y}
=
x^2+\frac{\partial C_1}{\partial y}
=
2yz+x^2.
Therefore,
\frac{\partial C_1}{\partial y}=2yz,
so
C_1(y,z)=y^2z+C_2(z).
Thus
\varphi(x,y,z)=x^2y-xz^2+y^2z+C_2(z).
Finally use the third component:
\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial z}
=
-2xz+y^2+C_2'(z).
This must equal
F_3=-2zx+y^2.
Hence C_2'(z)=0, so C_2 is constant. A potential is therefore
\boxed{\varphi(x,y,z)=x^2y+y^2z-xz^2+C.}
This is the main constructive method: integrate one component, keep a function of the remaining variables, and use the other components to determine that function.
A particularly simple three-dimensional example is
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=yz\,\mathbf{i}+zx\,\mathbf{j}+xy\,\mathbf{k}.
The components are
F_1=yz,
\qquad
F_2=zx,
\qquad
F_3=xy.
The mixed partial derivatives match:
\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial y}=z
=
\frac{\partial F_2}{\partial x},
\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial z}=y
=
\frac{\partial F_3}{\partial x},
and
\frac{\partial F_2}{\partial z}=x
=
\frac{\partial F_3}{\partial y}.
Since the field is defined on all of \mathbb{R}^3, it is conservative. A potential is easy to recognize:
\boxed{\varphi(x,y,z)=xyz+C.}
Indeed,
\nabla(xyz)=yz\,\mathbf{i}+xz\,\mathbf{j}+xy\,\mathbf{k}.
This example also connects conservative fields to field lines. A field line is a curve whose tangent direction at each point is parallel to the vector field at that point. For a vector field
\mathbf{F}=F_1\mathbf{i}+F_2\mathbf{j}+F_3\mathbf{k},
field lines may be described by
\frac{dx}{F_1}
=
\frac{dy}{F_2}
=
\frac{dz}{F_3},
where this notation means that the curve’s tangent vector is proportional to the field vector. For
\mathbf{F}=yz\,\mathbf{i}+zx\,\mathbf{j}+xy\,\mathbf{k},
the field-line equations are
\frac{dx}{yz}
=
\frac{dy}{zx}
=
\frac{dz}{xy}.
Comparing the first two fractions gives
\frac{dx}{yz}=\frac{dy}{zx}.
Cross-multiplying gives
zx\,dx=yz\,dy.
Away from special zero cases, this simplifies to
x\,dx=y\,dy.
Integrating,
\frac12x^2=\frac12y^2+C,
so
x^2-y^2=C_1.
Similarly, comparing the first and third fractions gives
x^2-z^2=C_2.
Therefore the field line through (x_0,y_0,z_0) is contained in the intersection of the two surfaces
x^2-y^2=x_0^2-y_0^2,
and
x^2-z^2=x_0^2-z_0^2.
This illustrates the difference between a potential and field lines: the potential \varphi=xyz gives scalar level surfaces, while the field lines are curves tangent to \nabla\varphi.
[Insert Figure 16.5 here: field lines and equipotential curves for \mathbf{F}=x\mathbf{i}-y\mathbf{j}. The figure should show one family of curves following the vector field and another family representing constant potential values.]
Equipotential curves and surfaces describe where the potential has the same value. If \mathbf{F}=\nabla\varphi, then a surface
\varphi(x,y,z)=C
is called an equipotential surface. In two dimensions, a curve
\varphi(x,y)=C
is called an equipotential curve. The word “equipotential” means that every point on the same curve or surface has the same value of the potential.
Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines. To see this, suppose a curve \mathbf{r}(t) lies on an equipotential surface. Then
\varphi(\mathbf{r}(t))=C
is constant. Differentiating with respect to t gives
\frac{d}{dt}\varphi(\mathbf{r}(t))
=
\nabla\varphi(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)
=
0.
Here \mathbf{r}'(t) is tangent to the curve lying on the equipotential surface. Since \nabla\varphi=\mathbf{F}, the vector field is perpendicular to tangent directions on the equipotential surface. Therefore the field lines cross equipotential surfaces at right angles, except at points where \mathbf{F}=\mathbf{0}, because there the field has no definite direction.
This gives a quick way to find a normal vector to an equipotential surface. If
\mathbf{F}=\nabla\varphi,
then \mathbf{F} is normal to the surface
\varphi(x,y,z)=C.
At a point where \mathbf{F}\neq\mathbf{0}, a unit normal vector is
\widehat{\mathbf{N}}
=
\pm\frac{\mathbf{F}}{|\mathbf{F}|}.
The sign depends on which orientation is requested. If no orientation is specified, both directions are normal.
For example, for
\mathbf{F}(x,y)=x\mathbf{i}-y\mathbf{j},
a potential is
\varphi(x,y)=\frac12x^2-\frac12y^2+C.
The equipotential curves are
\frac12x^2-\frac12y^2=C,
or equivalently
x^2-y^2=C_1.
These are hyperbolas. The field lines are found from
\frac{dx}{x}=\frac{dy}{-y}.
Integrating gives
\ln|x|=-\ln|y|+C,
so
xy=C_2.
Thus the equipotential curves are x^2-y^2=C_1, while the field lines are xy=C_2. The two families are not the same; they intersect orthogonally. This distinction is important. Field lines show the direction of the vector field. Equipotential curves show where the scalar potential is constant.
Conservative fields can also be recognized in polar coordinates, but the test looks different because the polar unit vectors and scale factors are different. In plane polar coordinates, the gradient of a scalar field \varphi(r,\theta) is
\nabla\varphi
=
\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial r}\widehat{\mathbf{r}}
+
\frac1r\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\theta}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}.
Here \widehat{\mathbf{r}} is the unit vector pointing radially outward, and \widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} is the unit vector in the direction of increasing angle. Suppose a polar vector field is written as
\mathbf{F}(r,\theta)
=
F_r(r,\theta)\widehat{\mathbf{r}}
+
F_\theta(r,\theta)\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}.
If this field is conservative, then
F_r=\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial r},
\qquad
F_\theta=\frac1r\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\theta}.
The second equation is equivalent to
rF_\theta=\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\theta}.
Now differentiate the first equation with respect to \theta:
\frac{\partial F_r}{\partial\theta}
=
\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial\theta\,\partial r}.
Differentiate the equation rF_\theta=\partial\varphi/\partial\theta with respect to r:
\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(rF_\theta)
=
\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial r\,\partial\theta}.
Since the mixed partial derivatives agree,
\frac{\partial F_r}{\partial\theta}
=
\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(rF_\theta).
Expanding the right-hand side gives
\frac{\partial F_r}{\partial\theta}
=
F_\theta+r\frac{\partial F_\theta}{\partial r}.
Therefore a necessary polar-coordinate condition for conservativeness is
\boxed{
\frac{\partial F_r}{\partial\theta}
=
r\frac{\partial F_\theta}{\partial r}
+
F_\theta.
}
This formula is a warning against applying the Cartesian test blindly in polar form. In Cartesian coordinates, one compares partial derivatives of Cartesian components. In polar coordinates, the components are measured along \widehat{\mathbf{r}} and \widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}, and the factor r in the gradient changes the condition.
There is also a differential notation for the same idea. If
\mathbf{F}
=
F_1\mathbf{i}+F_2\mathbf{j}+F_3\mathbf{k},
then the expression
F_1\,dx+F_2\,dy+F_3\,dz
is called a differential form of degree one in this context. If \mathbf{F}=\nabla\varphi, then
d\varphi
=
\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x}\,dx
+
\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial y}\,dy
+
\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial z}\,dz
=
F_1\,dx+F_2\,dy+F_3\,dz.
In that case, the differential form is called exact. Thus, saying that \mathbf{F} is conservative is equivalent to saying that F_1\,dx+F_2\,dy+F_3\,dz is the exact differential of a potential \varphi. This is the multivariable analogue of recognizing an expression as the derivative of something simpler.
[Insert point-source/equipotential figure here: field lines radiating from or into a point source, with equipotential circles or spheres centered on the source. The figure should support the connection between inverse-distance potentials, inverse-square fields, and perpendicular equipotentials.]
Many physical conservative fields arise from inverse-distance potentials. Let \mathbf{x} be the position vector of the point where the field is being measured, and let \mathbf{x}_0 be the position of a point source, mass, or charge. A typical potential has the form
\varphi(\mathbf{x})
=
\frac{Cq}{|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_0|},
where q is the strength of the source, C is a constant depending on the physical model and units, and |\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_0| is the distance from the source point. Differentiating this potential gives a field proportional to
\frac{\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_0}{|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_0|^3},
possibly with a minus sign depending on the convention. The magnitude of this vector is proportional to
\frac{1}{|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_0|^2}.
This is why inverse-distance potentials generate inverse-square fields. The singular source point \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}_0 must be excluded from the domain because the formula is undefined there.
If there are several sources or charges, potentials add. For point sources at \mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_n, a combined potential may be written as
\varphi(\mathbf{x})
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\frac{Cq_i}{|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_i|}.
Because the gradient is linear,
\nabla\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \varphi_i\right)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n \nabla\varphi_i.
Therefore the total field is the sum of the individual fields. This is one of the practical advantages of potentials: it is often easier to add scalar potentials first and then differentiate than to reason directly about the full vector field.
A source is a point from which field lines move outward. A sink is a point toward which field lines move inward. A dipole consists of a source and a sink of equal strength placed close together. The product of the source strength and the separation distance is called the dipole moment. Dipoles are useful because they show that even complicated-looking field-line patterns can come from scalar potentials. The key point for this section is not the full physical theory of dipoles, but the method: identify or construct the potential, then obtain the vector field by taking its gradient.
Conservative fields also simplify line integrals. A line integral of a vector field along a parametrized curve
\mathbf{r}(t)
=
x(t)\mathbf{i}+y(t)\mathbf{j}+z(t)\mathbf{k},
\qquad a\le t\le b,
is
\int_C\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}
=
\int_a^b
\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot\mathbf{r}'(t)\,dt.
This integral measures the accumulated tangential component of the vector field along the curve. If \mathbf{F} is a force field, it represents work.
If \mathbf{F}=\nabla\varphi, then the chain rule gives
\frac{d}{dt}\varphi(\mathbf{r}(t))
=
\nabla\varphi(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot\mathbf{r}'(t)
=
\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot\mathbf{r}'(t).
Therefore
\int_C\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}
=
\int_a^b
\frac{d}{dt}\varphi(\mathbf{r}(t))\,dt
=
\varphi(\mathbf{r}(b))-\varphi(\mathbf{r}(a)).
If C starts at P and ends at Q, this becomes
\boxed{
\int_C\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}
=
\varphi(Q)-\varphi(P).
}
Thus, for a conservative field, the vector line integral depends only on the endpoints, not on the path. If the curve is closed, then P=Q, and
\boxed{
\oint_C\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}=0.
}
This is the mathematical form of zero net work around a closed loop. It is also a practical shortcut: if a field is known to be conservative and a potential is known, do not compute a complicated parametrized line integral unless the problem explicitly asks for a direct computation. Use the potential difference.
The main ideas of this section fit together as follows. A conservative field is a vector field generated by the gradient of a scalar potential. To test conservativeness, compare cross-partials, but always pay attention to the domain. To find a potential, integrate one component at a time, remembering that integration constants may depend on the other variables. Equipotential curves and surfaces are level sets of the potential, and the vector field is normal to them. Field lines follow the vector field and therefore cross equipotentials at right angles. In physical force problems, the sign convention \mathbf{F}=-\nabla U must be handled carefully. Finally, conservative fields make line integrals depend only on endpoints, which is the computational payoff of the entire concept.

math-2/notes/16-3-line-integrals-1781625.title: 16.3 Line Integrals
math-2/notes/16-3-line-integrals-1781625.content:
16.3 Line Integrals
Integration has already been used to add quantities over intervals, plane regions, and solid regions. A single integral adds small pieces along a straight interval on the real line. A double integral adds small area contributions over a region in the plane. A triple integral adds small volume contributions throughout a solid in space. The new situation in this section is that the object over which we want to integrate is not a straight interval, an area, or a volume. It is a curve.
This problem appears naturally when a physical quantity is distributed along a thin curved object. A wire, for example, may be bent into a curve in space. If its density varies from point to point, then its mass is not found by multiplying one constant density by one length. Instead, the wire must be divided into many very small curve pieces. On each small piece, the density is approximately constant, so the mass of that piece is approximately
\text{density at the piece}\times \text{length of the piece}.
A line integral is the mathematical operation that performs this addition along a curve. The word “line” here does not mean that the path must be a straight line. It means that the integration takes place along a one-dimensional curve.
[Insert figure here: a curved wire in space divided into many short arc pieces. Label one short piece by ds, and label a point on the wire by \mathbf r(t). Indicate that a scalar value f(\mathbf r(t)), such as density, is attached to that point. This figure belongs here because it shows why the basic infinitesimal object in a scalar line integral is a small length along the curve.]
To integrate along a curve, we first need a way to describe the curve. Suppose \mathcal C is a curve in \mathbb R^3. A parametrization of \mathcal C is a vector-valued function
\mathbf r(t)=x(t)\mathbf i+y(t)\mathbf j+z(t)\mathbf k,\qquad a\leq t\leq b.
Here t is the parameter, \mathbf r(t) is the position vector of the point on the curve corresponding to t, and x(t), y(t), and z(t) are the coordinate functions of that point. The interval a\leq t\leq b tells us which part of the curve is traced. In the plane, the same idea is used with
\mathbf r(t)=x(t)\mathbf i+y(t)\mathbf j.
The derivative of the parametrization is
\mathbf r'(t)=\frac{d\mathbf r}{dt}=x'(t)\mathbf i+y'(t)\mathbf j+z'(t)\mathbf k.
This vector points tangent to the curve, in the direction in which the parametrization moves. Its length is
|\mathbf r'(t)|=\sqrt{(x'(t))^2+(y'(t))^2+(z'(t))^2}.
This quantity is the speed of the parametrization. Even when t is not literally time, |\mathbf r'(t)| tells us how much arc length is traced per unit change in t. Therefore a small change dt in the parameter corresponds to a small length
ds=|\mathbf r'(t)|\,dt
along the curve. The symbol ds means a small scalar arc-length element. It is not the same thing as dx, dy, dz, or dt. It is the actual distance measured along the curve.
A curve is called smooth on an interval if \mathbf r'(t) is continuous and nonzero there. The continuity condition prevents sudden jumps in the tangent direction, and the nonzero condition prevents the parametrization from stopping. A curve is called piecewise smooth if it can be split into finitely many smooth pieces. Line integrals over piecewise smooth curves are computed by integrating over each smooth piece and then adding the results.
Now let f(x,y,z) be a scalar field. A scalar field assigns one real number to each point in its domain. For example, f(x,y,z) could represent the density of a wire at the point (x,y,z). If the curve is parametrized by \mathbf r(t), then the value of the scalar field on the curve is
f(\mathbf r(t))=f(x(t),y(t),z(t)).
The scalar line integral of f along \mathcal C is written
\int_{\mathcal C} f(x,y,z)\,ds.
This notation means: add the scalar values of f along the curve, weighted by small pieces of arc length. Using the parametrization, the computational formula is
\int_{\mathcal C} f(x,y,z)\,ds=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))|\mathbf r'(t)|\,dt.
Here \mathbf r(t) is the parametrization of the curve for a\leq t\leq b, f(\mathbf r(t)) is the scalar field evaluated on the curve, and |\mathbf r'(t)|dt is the small length element ds. This formula is the main formula of scalar line integrals.
The formula can be understood directly from a Riemann-sum idea. Divide the parameter interval [a,b] into many small subintervals. Each subinterval corresponds to a short piece of the curve. If \Delta s_i denotes the length of the i-th small curve piece, and if t_i^* is a sample parameter value in that piece, then the contribution from that piece is approximately
f(\mathbf r(t_i^*))\,\Delta s_i.
Adding these contributions gives
\sum_i f(\mathbf r(t_i^*))\,\Delta s_i.
As the pieces become smaller and smaller, this sum approaches the line integral
\int_{\mathcal C}f\,ds.
Since a small length along the curve satisfies \Delta s\approx |\mathbf r'(t)|\Delta t, the limiting integral becomes
\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))|\mathbf r'(t)|\,dt.
This explains why the speed factor |\mathbf r'(t)| must appear. It is not optional. It converts the parameter increment dt into actual distance along the curve.
A particularly important special case is f=1. Then
\int_{\mathcal C}1\,ds=\int_a^b |\mathbf r'(t)|\,dt.
This is exactly the arc length of the curve. Thus scalar line integrals generalize arc length: instead of adding only length, they add length weighted by a scalar field.
If f represents density, then the mass of a wire lying along \mathcal C is
M=\int_{\mathcal C} f\,ds.
If the density is \delta(x,y,z), the mass formula is
M=\int_{\mathcal C}\delta(x,y,z)\,ds.
Here \delta(x,y,z) means mass per unit length at the point (x,y,z). The small mass element is
dm=\delta(x,y,z)\,ds.
Moments and centroids of wires are obtained in the same way. If a wire has density \delta(x,y,z), then its centroid coordinates are
\bar x=\frac{1}{M}\int_{\mathcal C}x\,\delta(x,y,z)\,ds,
\bar y=\frac{1}{M}\int_{\mathcal C}y\,\delta(x,y,z)\,ds,
\bar z=\frac{1}{M}\int_{\mathcal C}z\,\delta(x,y,z)\,ds.
In each formula, the numerator is a moment and M is the total mass. The factor x, y, or z measures how far the small mass element lies in the corresponding coordinate direction.
The value of a scalar line integral does not depend on the particular parametrization, as long as the parametrization traces the same curve once. However, the choice of parametrization can make the computation much easier or much harder. A good parametrization should fit the geometry of the curve. If the curve is a graph-like curve, it is often convenient to choose t=x or t=y. If the curve is a circle or ellipse, trigonometric functions are usually natural. If the curve is given as the intersection of two surfaces, the first task is to use the surface equations to build a one-parameter description of the curve.
As a simple example, consider the line segment from (1,1) to (3,2) in the plane, and compute
\int_{\mathcal C}(x^2+y^2)\,ds.
A convenient parametrization is
\mathbf r(t)=(1+2t)\mathbf i+(1+t)\mathbf j,\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1.
At t=0, this gives the starting point (1,1). At t=1, it gives the endpoint (3,2). The derivative is
\mathbf r'(t)=2\mathbf i+\mathbf j,
so
|\mathbf r'(t)|=\sqrt{2^2+1^2}=\sqrt5.
Along the curve,
x=1+2t,\qquad y=1+t.
Therefore
x^2+y^2=(1+2t)^2+(1+t)^2.
The line integral becomes
\int_{\mathcal C}(x^2+y^2)\,ds=\int_0^1\left((1+2t)^2+(1+t)^2\right)\sqrt5\,dt.
Expanding,
(1+2t)^2+(1+t)^2=2+6t+5t^2.
Thus
\int_{\mathcal C}(x^2+y^2)\,ds=\sqrt5\int_0^1(2+6t+5t^2)\,dt.
Evaluating the integral gives
\sqrt5\left[2t+3t^2+\frac53t^3\right]_0^1
=\sqrt5\left(2+3+\frac53\right)
=\frac{20\sqrt5}{3}.
The important step was not the final integration. The important step was converting the curve integral into an ordinary integral using
ds=|\mathbf r'(t)|dt.
A common error is to forget the speed factor. For the scalar line integral
\int_{\mathcal C}f\,ds,
the expression ds must become
|\mathbf r'(t)|dt.
It should not be replaced by \mathbf r'(t)dt, because \mathbf r'(t)dt is a vector displacement, not a scalar length.
[Insert figure here: the conical helix \mathbf r(t)=(t\cos t,t\sin t,t) for 0\leq t\leq2\pi, showing that the radius from the z-axis grows as t increases. This figure belongs here because the example tests the full scalar line-integral method: substitute into the scalar field and multiply by the speed.]
Consider the conical helix
\mathbf r(t)=t\cos t\,\mathbf i+t\sin t\,\mathbf j+t\,\mathbf k,
\qquad 0\leq t\leq 2\pi.
This curve winds once around the z-axis while moving upward and outward. Suppose first that we want the general scalar line integral
\int_{\mathcal C}\phi\,ds,
where \phi(x,y,z) is a scalar field. Along the curve,
x=t\cos t,\qquad y=t\sin t,\qquad z=t.
Therefore the scalar field on the curve is
\phi(\mathbf r(t))=\phi(t\cos t,t\sin t,t).
Next we compute the speed. Differentiating the parametrization gives
\mathbf r'(t)=(\cos t-t\sin t)\mathbf i+(\sin t+t\cos t)\mathbf j+\mathbf k.
Hence
|\mathbf r'(t)|=\sqrt{(\cos t-t\sin t)^2+(\sin t+t\cos t)^2+1}.
The first two squared terms simplify:
(\cos t-t\sin t)^2+(\sin t+t\cos t)^2=1+t^2.
Therefore
|\mathbf r'(t)|=\sqrt{t^2+2}.
So the scalar line integral is
\int_{\mathcal C}\phi\,ds=\int_0^{2\pi}\phi(t\cos t,t\sin t,t)\sqrt{t^2+2}\,dt.
This is often the expected final setup if the scalar field \phi is not specified further. If, for example, the scalar field is f(x,y,z)=z, then along the curve z=t, and the integral becomes
\int_{\mathcal C}z\,ds=\int_0^{2\pi}t\sqrt{t^2+2}\,dt.
Using u=t^2+2, so that du=2t\,dt, we obtain
\int_0^{2\pi}t\sqrt{t^2+2}\,dt
=\frac12\int_2^{4\pi^2+2}u^{1/2}\,du
=\frac13\left[(t^2+2)^{3/2}\right]_0^{2\pi}.
Thus
\int_{\mathcal C}z\,ds=\frac{(4\pi^2+2)^{3/2}-2\sqrt2}{3}.
This example shows the standard scalar-line-integral procedure in its most compact form: compute \mathbf r'(t), compute |\mathbf r'(t)|, substitute the parametrization into the scalar field, and integrate.
[Insert figure here: the curve formed by the intersection of the elliptic cylinder x^2+2y^2=1 and the plane z=y, restricted to y\geq0. Show the curve running from (-1,0,0) to (1,0,0). This figure belongs here because it illustrates the common situation where the curve is not given directly as \mathbf r(t), so the first task is to parametrize it.]
Now consider a curve described as the intersection of two surfaces:
x^2+2y^2=1,
z=y,
with y\geq0. This is a curve in three-dimensional space. Since it is given by two equations, it is not yet ready for a line integral. We first need a one-parameter parametrization.
The equation
x^2+2y^2=1
is an elliptic cylinder. A useful trigonometric parametrization is obtained by choosing
x=-\cos t.
Then
x^2=\cos^2t.
Substituting this into the cylinder equation gives
\cos^2t+2y^2=1.
Therefore
2y^2=1-\cos^2t=\sin^2t.
Since the curve is restricted to y\geq0, choose
y=\frac{\sin t}{\sqrt2}.
The condition y\geq0 is satisfied for
0\leq t\leq \pi.
The plane equation z=y then gives
z=\frac{\sin t}{\sqrt2}.
Thus a parametrization of the curve is
\mathbf r(t)=-\cos t\,\mathbf i+\frac{\sin t}{\sqrt2}\mathbf j+\frac{\sin t}{\sqrt2}\mathbf k,
\qquad 0\leq t\leq \pi.
At t=0, this gives (-1,0,0). At t=\pi, this gives (1,0,0). Differentiating,
\mathbf r'(t)=\sin t\,\mathbf i+\frac{\cos t}{\sqrt2}\mathbf j+\frac{\cos t}{\sqrt2}\mathbf k.
The speed is
|\mathbf r'(t)|
=\sqrt{\sin^2t+\frac{\cos^2t}{2}+\frac{\cos^2t}{2}}
=\sqrt{\sin^2t+\cos^2t}
=1.
Therefore
ds=dt.
This is a very convenient parametrization because the speed is exactly 1. The arc length of the curve is therefore
\int_{\mathcal C}1\,ds=\int_0^\pi 1\,dt=\pi.
More generally, for any scalar field f(x,y,z),
\int_{\mathcal C}f\,ds
=\int_0^\pi
f\left(-\cos t,\frac{\sin t}{\sqrt2},\frac{\sin t}{\sqrt2}\right)\,dt.
This example illustrates a crucial method: when a curve is given as an intersection of surfaces, do not start integrating immediately. First turn the curve into a parametrized curve.
Another common intersection-curve situation occurs when a curve lies on both
z=x^2
and
z=2-x^2-2y^2
in the first octant. The first octant condition means
x\geq0,\qquad y\geq0,\qquad z\geq0.
If the curve runs from (0,1,0) to (1,0,1), then x naturally runs from 0 to 1. Choose
x=t,\qquad 0\leq t\leq1.
From z=x^2, we get
z=t^2.
Substitute x=t and z=t^2 into the second surface:
t^2=2-t^2-2y^2.
Then
2y^2=2-2t^2,
so
y^2=1-t^2.
Since the curve is in the first octant, y\geq0, and therefore
y=\sqrt{1-t^2}.
Thus
\mathbf r(t)=t\,\mathbf i+\sqrt{1-t^2}\,\mathbf j+t^2\,\mathbf k,
\qquad 0\leq t\leq1.
If a wire lies along this curve with density
\delta(x,y,z)=xy,
then its mass is
M=\int_{\mathcal C}xy\,ds.
Along the curve,
xy=t\sqrt{1-t^2}.
Also,
\mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf i-\frac{t}{\sqrt{1-t^2}}\mathbf j+2t\,\mathbf k.
Therefore
|\mathbf r'(t)|=\sqrt{1+\frac{t^2}{1-t^2}+4t^2}.
The mass becomes
M=
\int_0^1
t\sqrt{1-t^2}
\sqrt{1+\frac{t^2}{1-t^2}+4t^2}\,dt.
The integrand simplifies to
t\sqrt{1+4t^2-4t^4},
so
M=\int_0^1t\sqrt{1+4t^2-4t^4}\,dt.
The most important part of this example is the parametrization step. The density and the speed are evaluated only after the curve has been written as \mathbf r(t).
Scalar line integrals are not oriented. This means that if a curve is traversed in the opposite direction, the value of
\int_{\mathcal C} f\,ds
does not change. The reason is that ds is a positive length element. Reversing direction changes the sign of the velocity vector \mathbf r'(t), but it does not change its length |\mathbf r'(t)|. Scalar line integrals measure accumulated amount along the curve, not signed motion along the curve.
This is the point where another kind of line integral enters. Scalar line integrals use ds, a scalar length element. Vector fields require a different object. Suppose \mathbf F(x,y,z) is a vector field. At each point, \mathbf F assigns a vector. If \mathbf F is a force field and a particle moves along a curve, then only the part of the force pointing along the motion contributes to work. A force perpendicular to the motion may be large, but it does no work along that motion.
[Insert figure here: a curve \mathcal C, a tangent vector \mathbf r'(t), a unit tangent vector \mathbf T(t), and a force vector \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) making an angle with the tangent. Show that the tangential component is measured by a dot product. This figure belongs here because it explains why vector line integrals use \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r.]
The displacement vector along the curve is
d\mathbf r=\mathbf r'(t)\,dt.
This is different from ds. The quantity d\mathbf r has direction, while ds is only length. For a vector field \mathbf F, the vector line integral along \mathcal C is
\int_{\mathcal C}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r.
If the curve is parametrized by \mathbf r(t), a\leq t\leq b, then
\int_{\mathcal C}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r
=\int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,dt.
Here \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) is the vector field evaluated on the curve, and \mathbf r'(t) is the tangent velocity vector of the curve. The dot product selects the component of \mathbf F in the direction of the curve.
This formula can also be understood from a Riemann sum. Divide the curve into small directed displacement vectors
\Delta\mathbf r_i=\mathbf r(t_i)-\mathbf r(t_{i-1}).
On the i-th small piece, the vector field is approximately \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t_i^*)). The contribution is approximately
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t_i^*))\cdot \Delta\mathbf r_i.
Adding over all pieces gives
\sum_i \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t_i^*))\cdot \Delta\mathbf r_i.
As the pieces become smaller, this sum approaches
\int_{\mathcal C}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r.
This explains why vector line integrals use d\mathbf r, not ds. The vector displacement carries the direction of travel.
If
\mathbf F(x,y,z)=F_1(x,y,z)\mathbf i+F_2(x,y,z)\mathbf j+F_3(x,y,z)\mathbf k,
and
\mathbf r(t)=x(t)\mathbf i+y(t)\mathbf j+z(t)\mathbf k,
then
\mathbf r'(t)=x'(t)\mathbf i+y'(t)\mathbf j+z'(t)\mathbf k.
Thus
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot \mathbf r'(t)
=F_1(\mathbf r(t))x'(t)
+F_2(\mathbf r(t))y'(t)
+F_3(\mathbf r(t))z'(t).
So the vector line integral becomes
\int_{\mathcal C}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r
=\int_a^b
\left[
F_1(\mathbf r(t))x'(t)
+F_2(\mathbf r(t))y'(t)
+F_3(\mathbf r(t))z'(t)
\right]dt.
This is often written in differential notation as
\int_{\mathcal C}F_1\,dx+F_2\,dy+F_3\,dz.
This notation means
dx=x'(t)\,dt,\qquad dy=y'(t)\,dt,\qquad dz=z'(t)\,dt.
It does not mean that dx, dy, and dz are chosen independently. They are all determined by the same parametrized curve.
The distinction between the two kinds of line integrals is essential:
\int_{\mathcal C} f\,ds
=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))|\mathbf r'(t)|\,dt
is a scalar line integral, while
\int_{\mathcal C}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r
=\int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,dt
is a vector line integral. In the first formula, the curve contributes its speed |\mathbf r'(t)|. In the second formula, the curve contributes its velocity vector \mathbf r'(t). Reversing the direction of the curve leaves the scalar line integral unchanged, but it changes the sign of the vector line integral.
For the earlier intersection curve
\mathbf r(t)=-\cos t\,\mathbf i+\frac{\sin t}{\sqrt2}\mathbf j+\frac{\sin t}{\sqrt2}\mathbf k,
\qquad 0\leq t\leq \pi,
the derivative is
\mathbf r'(t)=\sin t\,\mathbf i+\frac{\cos t}{\sqrt2}\mathbf j+\frac{\cos t}{\sqrt2}\mathbf k.
Therefore, for a vector field \mathbf F,
\int_{\mathcal C}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r
=\int_0^\pi
\mathbf F\left(-\cos t,\frac{\sin t}{\sqrt2},\frac{\sin t}{\sqrt2}\right)
\cdot
\left(
\sin t\,\mathbf i
+\frac{\cos t}{\sqrt2}\mathbf j
+\frac{\cos t}{\sqrt2}\mathbf k
\right)
dt.
Compare this with the scalar formula for the same curve:
\int_{\mathcal C}f\,ds
=\int_0^\pi
f\left(-\cos t,\frac{\sin t}{\sqrt2},\frac{\sin t}{\sqrt2}\right)dt.
The curve is the same, but the integrals use different curve factors. The scalar integral uses the speed, which here equals 1. The vector integral uses the full tangent vector.
If a curve \mathcal C is closed, meaning that it starts and ends at the same point, then a vector line integral around it is often written
\oint_{\mathcal C}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r.
The circle on the integral sign indicates that the curve is closed. Such an integral is called the circulation of \mathbf F around \mathcal C. Circulation measures the net tendency of the vector field to push in the direction of travel around the closed curve.
[Insert figure here: the vector field \mathbf F(x,y)=\frac{-y\mathbf i+x\mathbf j}{x^2+y^2}, with arrows tangent to circles around the origin. Show a counterclockwise circle and a counterclockwise square surrounding the origin. This figure belongs here because it clarifies circulation, orientation, and the importance of singular points.]
Consider the vector field
\mathbf F(x,y)=\frac{-y\mathbf i+x\mathbf j}{x^2+y^2}.
This field is defined everywhere in the plane except at the origin, where the denominator x^2+y^2 is zero. The vectors circulate around the origin. We compute the circulation around the circle
x^2+y^2=2
traversed counterclockwise. A convenient parametrization is
\mathbf r(\theta)=\sqrt2\cos\theta\,\mathbf i+\sqrt2\sin\theta\,\mathbf j,
\qquad -\frac{\pi}{4}\leq \theta\leq \frac{7\pi}{4}.
This starts at (1,-1) and makes one full counterclockwise revolution. The derivative is
\mathbf r'(\theta)=-\sqrt2\sin\theta\,\mathbf i+\sqrt2\cos\theta\,\mathbf j.
On the circle,
x^2+y^2=2,
so
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(\theta))=\frac{-\sqrt2\sin\theta\,\mathbf i+\sqrt2\cos\theta\,\mathbf j}{2}.
Therefore
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(\theta))\cdot\mathbf r'(\theta)=1.
Thus
\oint_{\mathcal C}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r
=\int_{-\pi/4}^{7\pi/4}1\,d\theta
=2\pi.
The same value is obtained if the circle is replaced by the square [-1,1]\times[-1,1], oriented counterclockwise. The computation can be done by splitting the square into four line segments. Each side contributes \pi/2, so the total is again
2\pi.
The important point is not that every closed curve gives 2\pi. The important point is that this vector field measures angular circulation around the origin. A closed curve going once counterclockwise around the origin gives total circulation 2\pi. If the same curve were traversed clockwise, the answer would be -2\pi. Direction matters for vector line integrals.
This example also warns against a common mistake. Away from the origin, the field has a local structure that resembles a gradient of an angle function, but the origin is missing from the domain. The missing point matters. One cannot ignore points where the vector field is not defined, especially when a curve surrounds such a point.
The connection with conservative fields gives an important shortcut, but only when its conditions are satisfied. If a vector field \mathbf F is the gradient of a scalar potential \phi, so that
\mathbf F=\nabla\phi,
then \mathbf F is conservative. For a conservative field,
\int_{\mathcal C}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r
=\phi(\mathbf r(b))-\phi(\mathbf r(a)).
Here \mathbf r(a) is the starting point of the curve and \mathbf r(b) is the endpoint. This formula says that the vector line integral depends only on the endpoints, not on the path taken between them.
For example, let
\mathbf F(x,y)=y^2\mathbf i+2xy\mathbf j.
This field is the gradient of
\phi(x,y)=xy^2,
because
\nabla\phi
=\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x}\mathbf i
+\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial y}\mathbf j
=y^2\mathbf i+2xy\mathbf j.
Therefore, for any path from (0,0) to (1,1),
\int_{\mathcal C}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r
=\phi(1,1)-\phi(0,0)
=1\cdot1^2-0
=1.
This shortcut should not replace the basic method. The basic method is always to parametrize the curve and compute
\int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)\,dt.
The conservative-field shortcut is available only after a valid potential has been identified on the relevant domain.
The practical method for line integrals can now be summarized in words. First determine which type of line integral is being asked. If the integral has the form
\int_{\mathcal C}f\,ds,
it is a scalar line integral, so the curve contributes the speed |\mathbf r'(t)|. If the integral has the form
\int_{\mathcal C}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r
or
\int_{\mathcal C}P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz,
it is a vector line integral, so the curve contributes the tangent vector \mathbf r'(t). Next, parametrize the curve with correct bounds. Then substitute the parametrization into the scalar or vector field. Finally, integrate over the parameter interval. If the curve is piecewise smooth, do this separately on each piece and add the results.
Line integrals extend integration to curved one-dimensional objects. The scalar line integral
\int_{\mathcal C}f\,ds
adds a scalar quantity along a curve and is used for length, mass, moments, and centroids of wires. The vector line integral
\int_{\mathcal C}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r
adds the tangential contribution of a vector field along an oriented curve and is used for work and circulation. Both are reduced to ordinary one-variable integrals by parametrizing the curve. The central distinction is that ds is a positive length element, while d\mathbf r is a directed displacement. Remembering this distinction prevents most mistakes in this section.

math-2/notes/16-5-surfaces-and-surface-i.title: 16.5 Surfaces and Surface Integrals
math-2/notes/16-5-surfaces-and-surface-i.content:
16.5 Surfaces and Surface Integrals
In the previous parts of the course, integration was extended step by step from intervals to larger geometric objects. A single integral adds up a quantity along an interval. A double integral adds up a quantity over a flat two-dimensional region. A triple integral adds up a quantity throughout a three-dimensional solid. A line integral adds up a quantity along a curve. The next natural object is a curved two-dimensional surface in three-dimensional space, such as a sphere, cone, cylinder, paraboloid, shell, membrane, or graph z=f(x,y).
The problem solved in this section is the following: how do we add up a scalar quantity that is spread over a curved surface? For example, if a thin curved sheet has density depending on position, then its total mass is obtained by adding density times small pieces of surface area. If the scalar quantity is simply 1, then the same integral gives the area of the surface itself. The new difficulty is not the idea of integration, but the correct expression for a small piece of curved surface area.
A surface integral is therefore the surface analogue of a double integral. The difference is that the domain of integration is not necessarily a flat region in the xy-plane. It may bend through three-dimensional space. To handle this, we describe the surface using parameters and then convert the integral over the curved surface into an ordinary double integral over a flat parameter domain.

A curve is one-dimensional, so one parameter is usually enough to describe it. A surface is two-dimensional, so two parameters are usually needed. A parametric surface is a vector-valued function of two variables,
\mathbf r(u,v)=x(u,v)\mathbf i+y(u,v)\mathbf j+z(u,v)\mathbf k.
The parameters u and v range over a region \mathcal D in the uv-plane. The function \mathbf r sends each pair (u,v) to the point
(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v))
in three-dimensional space. The region \mathcal D is called the parameter domain. The surface S is the set of points traced out by \mathbf r(u,v) as (u,v) moves through \mathcal D.
A simple example is the graph of a function z=g(x,y). Since the height z is already determined by the two coordinates x and y, we can use x and y themselves as parameters:
\mathbf r(x,y)=x\mathbf i+y\mathbf j+g(x,y)\mathbf k.
Here the parameter domain is the domain of g in the xy-plane. This parametrization says: start from a point (x,y) in the base region, then move vertically to the height z=g(x,y).
A sphere gives a different type of example. The sphere of radius a centred at the origin can be parametrized by
\mathbf r(\phi,\theta)=a\sin\phi\cos\theta\,\mathbf i+a\sin\phi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j+a\cos\phi\,\mathbf k,
where 0\leq \phi\leq \pi and 0\leq \theta\leq 2\pi. The parameter \phi is the angle measured down from the positive z-axis, and \theta is the angle around the z-axis. If 0\leq \phi\leq \pi/2, the parametrization covers only the upper hemisphere. This example is important because a sphere cannot be represented globally as one graph z=g(x,y), but it can still be represented naturally as a parametric surface.
An ellipsoid can be parametrized in the same spirit. The surface
\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}+\frac{z^2}{c^2}=1
may be described by
\mathbf r(u,v)=a\cos u\sin v\,\mathbf i+b\sin u\sin v\,\mathbf j+c\cos v\,\mathbf k,
where 0\leq u\leq 2\pi and 0\leq v\leq \pi. The formula is a stretched version of the spherical parametrization: the x-coordinate is scaled by a, the y-coordinate by b, and the z-coordinate by c.
A parametrization is not unique. The same surface can often be parametrized in several different ways. What matters is that the chosen parametrization describes the surface correctly and covers it once, except possibly along boundary curves. If a parametrization covers the same surface twice, then a surface integral computed from it will usually count the surface twice. Therefore the parameter bounds are part of the mathematics, not just a technical detail. When angles are used, one must always check whether the interval traces the surface once or repeats it.
A surface can also be built from several smooth pieces. Such a surface is called piecewise smooth. The surface of a cube, for example, consists of six flat square faces. A cone together with its base consists of a curved lateral surface and a flat disk. For scalar surface integrals, the rule is simple: integrate over each smooth piece and add the results. No new principle is needed; the surface is just split into simpler pieces.

To integrate over a surface, we need a formula for a small piece of surface area. Suppose
\mathbf r(u,v)=x(u,v)\mathbf i+y(u,v)\mathbf j+z(u,v)\mathbf k
parametrizes a surface. If we change u while keeping v fixed, we move along a curve on the surface. The tangent vector in that direction is
\mathbf r_u=\frac{\partial \mathbf r}{\partial u}.
If we change v while keeping u fixed, we move along another curve on the surface. The tangent vector in that direction is
\mathbf r_v=\frac{\partial \mathbf r}{\partial v}.
For a very small rectangle du\,dv in the parameter plane, the corresponding surface patch is approximately a parallelogram spanned by the vectors \mathbf r_u\,du and \mathbf r_v\,dv. The area of a parallelogram spanned by two vectors is the magnitude of their cross product. Therefore the surface area element is
dS=\left|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right|\,du\,dv.
Here dS means a small area on the actual curved surface. The symbol du\,dv means a small flat area in the parameter domain. The factor
\left|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right|
converts parameter-area into true surface-area. This is the central formula of the section.
It is important that the magnitude is used. The cross product \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v is a vector, but a scalar surface integral needs an area, and area cannot be negative. Thus the scalar area factor is
\left|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right|,
not merely \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v. In this section, the direction of the cross product is not part of the scalar integral; only its length is used.
The cross product can be computed by the determinant
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=
\begin{vmatrix}
\mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k\\
x_u & y_u & z_u\\
x_v & y_v & z_v
\end{vmatrix}.
Here
x_u=\frac{\partial x}{\partial u},\qquad
 y_u=\frac{\partial y}{\partial u},\qquad
 z_u=\frac{\partial z}{\partial u},
and similarly x_v,y_v,z_v are the partial derivatives with respect to v. Equivalently,
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=
\frac{\partial(y,z)}{\partial(u,v)}\mathbf i
+
\frac{\partial(z,x)}{\partial(u,v)}\mathbf j
+
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\mathbf k.
This form shows that surface area is closely related to Jacobian determinants. A small parameter rectangle is stretched into a small surface parallelogram, and the cross product measures the amount of stretching.
Now let f(x,y,z) be a scalar function defined on a surface S. The scalar surface integral of f over S is written
\iint_S f(x,y,z)\,dS.
The meaning is: split the surface into tiny pieces, evaluate f on each piece, multiply by the area of that piece, and add the contributions. If S is parametrized by \mathbf r(u,v) over the parameter domain \mathcal D, then
\iint_S f(x,y,z)\,dS
=
\iint_{\mathcal D}
f(\mathbf r(u,v))
\left|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right|
\,du\,dv.
In this formula, f(\mathbf r(u,v)) means that x,y,z are replaced by x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v). The integral on the left is over the curved surface, while the integral on the right is an ordinary double integral over the flat parameter domain.
This formula includes surface area as a special case. If f=1, then
\iint_S 1\,dS=\iint_S dS
is the area of S. If f=\sigma(x,y,z), where \sigma is an areal density, then
\iint_S \sigma(x,y,z)\,dS
gives the total mass or total charge distributed over a thin surface, depending on what \sigma represents. If f=x^2+y^2, then the integral over a shell measures a rotational quantity about the z-axis when the surface has unit areal density.

The most important special case is a graph
z=g(x,y).
Parametrize the graph by
\mathbf r(x,y)=x\mathbf i+y\mathbf j+g(x,y)\mathbf k.
Then
\mathbf r_x=(1,0,g_x),
\qquad
\mathbf r_y=(0,1,g_y),
where
g_x=\frac{\partial g}{\partial x},
\qquad
g_y=\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}.
Their cross product is
\mathbf r_x\times\mathbf r_y=(-g_x,-g_y,1),
so its magnitude is
\left|\mathbf r_x\times\mathbf r_y\right|=
\sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}.
Therefore, for a graph z=g(x,y) over a domain D in the xy-plane,
dS=\sqrt{1+g_x(x,y)^2+g_y(x,y)^2}\,dx\,dy.
The surface integral becomes
\iint_S f(x,y,z)\,dS
=
\iint_D
f(x,y,g(x,y))
\sqrt{1+g_x(x,y)^2+g_y(x,y)^2}
\,dx\,dy.
This formula has a simple geometric meaning. If the surface is horizontal, then g_x=g_y=0, so
dS=dx\,dy.
The surface patch has the same area as its projection. If the surface is tilted, then
\sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}>1,
so the true surface area is larger than the projected area in the xy-plane.
The expression dx\,dy is not the same as dS. The symbol dx\,dy measures area in the flat xy-plane. The symbol dS measures area on the curved surface. The factor
\sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}
is precisely the correction from projected flat area to actual surface area.
A useful exam-style surface is
S=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:x^2-2x+y^2=z^2,\ 0\leq z\leq 1\}.
Before parametrizing, rewrite the equation by completing the square:
x^2-2x+y^2=z^2
becomes
(x-1)^2+y^2=1+z^2.
For each fixed z, this is a circle in the xy-plane centred at (1,0) with radius
\sqrt{1+z^2}.
Let u be the angle around this circle, and let v=z. Then a natural parametrization is
\mathbf r(u,v)=
\left(1+\sqrt{1+v^2}\cos u\right)\mathbf i
+
\sqrt{1+v^2}\sin u\,\mathbf j
+
v\mathbf k,
where
0\leq u\leq 2\pi,
\qquad
0\leq v\leq 1.
This parametrization is not guessed blindly. The shift 1 in the x-coordinate comes from the centre (1,0), the radius \sqrt{1+v^2} comes from the rewritten equation, u moves around the circle, and v moves through the allowed height interval.
To compute its area, write
R(v)=\sqrt{1+v^2}.
Then
\mathbf r_u=(-R\sin u,\ R\cos u,\ 0),
and
\mathbf r_v=
\left(\frac{v}{R}\cos u,\ \frac{v}{R}\sin u,\ 1\right).
The cross product is
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=(R\cos u,\ R\sin u,\ -v).
Therefore,
\left|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right|
=
\sqrt{R^2\cos^2u+R^2\sin^2u+v^2}
=
\sqrt{R^2+v^2}.
Since R^2=1+v^2, this becomes
\left|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right|=
\sqrt{1+2v^2}.
Thus the surface area is
\operatorname{Area}(S)
=
\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1
\sqrt{1+2v^2}\,dv\,du.
Because the integrand does not depend on u, this simplifies to
\operatorname{Area}(S)
=
2\pi\int_0^1\sqrt{1+2v^2}\,dv.
This is the expected final form if the problem asks for the answer as a constant times a one-variable integral. The essential work is setting up the parametrization correctly and finding the surface element.
The same surface can also be treated as a graph if one solves for z. Since
z=\sqrt{x^2-2x+y^2}
on the upper part of the surface, the graph formula can be used over the corresponding projection domain in the xy-plane. This gives the same answer when the projection and bounds are chosen correctly. In practice, the parametrization above is often cleaner because the cross-sections are circles.
A second way to obtain dS applies when a surface is given implicitly by an equation
G(x,y,z)=0.
Suppose the surface projects one-to-one onto a domain D in the xy-plane, and suppose
G_z=\frac{\partial G}{\partial z}\neq 0
on the surface. The gradient
\nabla G=(G_x,G_y,G_z)
is perpendicular to the level surface G=0. This fact gives the surface area element
dS=
\frac{|\nabla G(x,y,z)|}{|G_z(x,y,z)|}\,dx\,dy.
Here
|\nabla G|=
\sqrt{G_x^2+G_y^2+G_z^2}.
The denominator is |G_z| because the surface is being projected onto the xy-plane. If the surface is projected onto the xz-plane, the corresponding denominator is |G_y|. If the surface is projected onto the yz-plane, the denominator is |G_x|.
The corresponding scalar surface integral is
\iint_S f(x,y,z)\,dS
=
\iint_D
f(x,y,z)
\frac{|\nabla G(x,y,z)|}{|G_z(x,y,z)|}
\,dx\,dy,
where z is understood as the value on the surface. This formula is useful when the surface equation is easier to use than an explicit parametrization.
For example, consider the cone
z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}
between z=0 and z=1. Since this is already a graph, let
g(x,y)=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}.
On the cone,
g_x=\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}=\frac{x}{z},
\qquad
g_y=\frac{y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}=\frac{y}{z}.
The graph formula gives
dS=
\sqrt{1+\frac{x^2}{z^2}+\frac{y^2}{z^2}}\,dx\,dy.
Because z^2=x^2+y^2 on the cone,
\frac{x^2+y^2}{z^2}=1,
so
dS=\sqrt{2}\,dx\,dy.

If we want to compute
\iint_S z\,dS
over the part of the cone with 0\leq z\leq 1, the projection onto the xy-plane is the disk
x^2+y^2\leq 1.
On the cone, z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. In polar coordinates,
z=r,
\qquad
 dx\,dy=r\,dr\,d\theta.
Therefore,
\iint_S z\,dS
=
\sqrt{2}\iint_{x^2+y^2\leq 1} z\,dx\,dy
becomes
\iint_S z\,dS
=
\sqrt{2}
\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1
r\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta.
The first r is the value of z on the cone. The second r comes from the polar area element dx\,dy=r\,dr\,d\theta. Thus
\iint_S z\,dS
=
\sqrt{2}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 r^2\,dr\,d\theta
=
\frac{2\pi\sqrt2}{3}.
This example is a useful warning. When polar coordinates are used, an r may come from the function being integrated, from the surface equation, or from the polar area element. These roles must not be confused.
For spherical surfaces, there is a standard surface area element. On the sphere
R=a,
we may use the spherical parametrization
x=a\sin\phi\cos\theta,
\qquad
y=a\sin\phi\sin\theta,
\qquad
z=a\cos\phi.
The surface area element is
dS=a^2\sin\phi\,d\phi\,d\theta.
This is different from the spherical volume element
dV=R^2\sin\phi\,dR\,d\phi\,d\theta.
The distinction is essential. On the sphere R=a, the radius is fixed, so there is no dR. The element dS measures a thin surface; the element dV measures a solid volume.
As an example, consider the surface integral
\iint_S z^2\,dS
over the upper hemisphere
z=\sqrt{a^2-x^2-y^2}.
On the sphere,
z=a\cos\phi,
and over the upper hemisphere the bounds are
0\leq \theta\leq 2\pi,
\qquad
0\leq \phi\leq \frac{\pi}{2}.
Using
dS=a^2\sin\phi\,d\phi\,d\theta,
we obtain
\iint_S z^2\,dS
=
\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}
a^2\cos^2\phi\cdot a^2\sin\phi
\,d\phi\,d\theta.
Thus
\iint_S z^2\,dS
=
2\pi a^4\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2\phi\sin\phi\,d\phi.
Let
w=\cos\phi,
\qquad
dw=-\sin\phi\,d\phi.
When \phi=0, w=1, and when \phi=\pi/2, w=0. Therefore,
\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2\phi\sin\phi\,d\phi
=
\int_0^1 w^2\,dw
=
\frac13.
Hence
\iint_S z^2\,dS
=
\frac{2\pi a^4}{3}.
The same spherical element can be used for the moment of inertia of a uniform spherical shell about the z-axis. For unit areal density, the relevant integral is
\iint_S (x^2+y^2)\,dS.
On the sphere x^2+y^2+z^2=a^2,
x^2+y^2=a^2\sin^2\phi,
so
\iint_S (x^2+y^2)\,dS
=
\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi
a^2\sin^2\phi\cdot a^2\sin\phi
\,d\phi\,d\theta.
Thus
\iint_S (x^2+y^2)\,dS
=
2\pi a^4\int_0^\pi \sin^3\phi\,d\phi.
Since
\int_0^\pi \sin^3\phi\,d\phi=\frac43,
we get
\iint_S (x^2+y^2)\,dS
=
\frac{8\pi a^4}{3}.
If the shell has constant areal density \sigma, then the moment of inertia is multiplied by \sigma.

Sometimes the most efficient method is not to compute a full cross product. If the geometry gives the area element directly, use it. Consider the part of the cylinder
x^2+y^2=2ay
that lies inside the sphere
x^2+y^2+z^2=4a^2.
The cylinder is generated by vertical lines above the circle
x^2+y^2=2ay
in the xy-plane. In polar coordinates, this circle becomes
r^2=2ar\sin\theta,
so, away from the origin,
r=2a\sin\theta.
On the sphere, the positive height is
z=\sqrt{4a^2-r^2}.
A vertical strip on the cylinder has area equal to height times a small arc-length element along the base curve. Thus, on the upper half,
dS=z\,ds.
The polar arc-length element for a plane curve r=r(\theta) is
ds=
\sqrt{r^2+\left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2}\,d\theta.
For
r=2a\sin\theta,
we have
\frac{dr}{d\theta}=2a\cos\theta.
Therefore,
ds
=
\sqrt{4a^2\sin^2\theta+4a^2\cos^2\theta}\,d\theta
=
2a\,d\theta.
One quarter of the total cylindrical surface lies in the first octant. By symmetry, the total area is four times the first-octant area:
A
=
4\int_0^{\pi/2}
\sqrt{4a^2-r^2}\,2a\,d\theta.
Substituting r=2a\sin\theta, we get
A
=
4\int_0^{\pi/2}
\sqrt{4a^2-4a^2\sin^2\theta}\,2a\,d\theta.
Since
\sqrt{4a^2(1-\sin^2\theta)}
=
2a\cos\theta
on 0\leq\theta\leq\pi/2, this becomes
A
=
4\int_0^{\pi/2}
2a\cos\theta\cdot 2a\,d\theta
=
16a^2\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos\theta\,d\theta.
Therefore,
A=16a^2.
This example shows that dS does not always have to be found by memorized formulas. It can often be built from simpler geometric pieces: here, height times arc length.
A final example combines the graph formula with polar-coordinate bounds. Suppose
S=\{(x,y,z):(x,y)\in D,\ z=4-x^2-y^2\},
where
D=\{(x,y):2y\leq x^2+y^2\leq 4,\ x\geq 0,\ y\geq 0\}.
Let the scalar density on the surface be
\rho(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}.
The total amount on the surface is
\iint_S \rho\,dS.
Because this is a graph with
g(x,y)=4-x^2-y^2,
we compute
g_x=-2x,
\qquad
g_y=-2y.
Hence
dS=\sqrt{1+4x^2+4y^2}\,dx\,dy.
Now use polar coordinates in the projection domain:
x=r\cos\theta,
\qquad
y=r\sin\theta.
Then
\rho=\frac{r\cos\theta}{r^2}=\frac{\cos\theta}{r},
and
dS=\sqrt{1+4r^2}\,dx\,dy
=
\sqrt{1+4r^2}\,r\,dr\,d\theta.
Therefore,
\rho\,dS
=
\cos\theta\sqrt{1+4r^2}\,dr\,d\theta.
The conditions x\geq0 and y\geq0 give
0\leq\theta\leq\frac{\pi}{2}.
The condition x^2+y^2\leq 4 gives
r\leq 2.
The condition
2y\leq x^2+y^2
becomes
2r\sin\theta\leq r^2.
For r>0, this is
r\geq 2\sin\theta.
Thus one valid setup is
\iint_S \rho\,dS
=
\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_{2\sin\theta}^{2}
\cos\theta\sqrt{1+4r^2}\,dr\,d\theta.
The order can be improved by describing the same region using r first. Since
r\geq 2\sin\theta
is equivalent to
\sin\theta\leq\frac r2,
we can write
0\leq r\leq 2,
\qquad
0\leq \theta\leq \arcsin\left(\frac r2\right).
Then
\iint_S \rho\,dS
=
\int_0^2\int_0^{\arcsin(r/2)}
\cos\theta\sqrt{1+4r^2}\,d\theta\,dr.
The inner integral is now simple:
\int_0^{\arcsin(r/2)}\cos\theta\,d\theta
=
\sin\left(\arcsin\frac r2\right)
=
\frac r2.
Therefore,
\iint_S \rho\,dS
=
\frac12\int_0^2 r\sqrt{1+4r^2}\,dr.
Let
w=1+4r^2,
\qquad
dw=8r\,dr.
Then
\frac12 r\,dr=\frac{1}{16}\,dw.
When r=0, w=1. When r=2, w=17. Hence
\iint_S \rho\,dS
=
\frac{1}{16}\int_1^{17}w^{1/2}\,dw
=
\frac{1}{16}\cdot\frac{2}{3}w^{3/2}\Big|_1^{17}.
Thus
\iint_S \rho\,dS
=
\frac{1}{24}\left(17^{3/2}-1\right).
This example illustrates the full surface-integral workflow. First identify the surface type. Then find dS. Then rewrite the scalar quantity on the surface. Then describe the correct parameter or projection domain. Finally, choose bounds that make the integral as simple as possible.
The central idea of this section is that a curved surface can be integrated over by flattening its description into two parameters. The parametrization produces two tangent vectors, and the magnitude of their cross product gives the conversion from parameter area to true surface area. For graphs, this becomes the familiar correction factor \sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}. For implicit surfaces, the gradient gives an efficient projection formula. For spheres and cylinders, symmetry often provides especially simple area elements. In every case, the goal is the same: express dS correctly, express the scalar function on the surface, and integrate over a two-dimensional domain that covers the surface exactly once.

math-2/notes/adams-10-1-analytic-geometr.title: 10.1 Analytic Geometry in Three Dimensions
math-2/notes/adams-10-1-analytic-geometr.content:
Adams 10.1 — Analytic Geometry in Three Dimensions
The first problem in multivariable calculus is not differentiation or integration. It is description. In one-variable calculus, the input of a function is usually one real number, so the geometry is the geometry of the real line. A point is just a number x, intervals describe domains, and graphs live in the plane. In Math 2, the objects are spatial. A temperature field may depend on position (x,y,z), a particle may move through three-dimensional space, an electric field may assign a vector to every point in a region, and an integral may be taken over a surface or a solid. Before any of these ideas can be treated carefully, we need a language for locating points, measuring distances, describing surfaces, and deciding whether points lie inside, outside, or on the boundary of a region.
This is the purpose of analytic geometry in three dimensions. The word analytic means that geometry is described by equations and inequalities. Instead of only drawing a sphere, a plane, or a cylinder, we represent it by algebraic conditions on coordinates. This is why Adams 10.1 appears at the beginning of the course: it supplies the coordinate language needed for quadric surfaces, cylindrical and spherical coordinates, vector functions, parametrized curves, functions of several variables, multiple integrals, and vector fields.

Three-dimensional Cartesian space is built from three mutually perpendicular coordinate axes. These are called the x-axis, the y-axis, and the z-axis. The point where all three axes meet is called the origin and is denoted by O. A point P in space is described by an ordered triple
P=(x,y,z).
Here x, y, and z are real numbers. The number x tells how far the point is displaced in the x-direction, the number y tells how far it is displaced in the y-direction, and the number z tells how far it is displaced in the z-direction. The order matters: (1,2,3), (2,1,3), and (3,2,1) are generally different points.
The coordinate axes are oriented by the right-hand rule. This means that the positive x-, y-, and z-directions are arranged like the thumb, index finger, and middle finger of the right hand when placed in the standard orientation. In vector notation, the standard unit vectors are denoted by
\mathbf i,\qquad \mathbf j,\qquad \mathbf k.
The vector \mathbf i points in the positive x-direction, \mathbf j points in the positive y-direction, and \mathbf k points in the positive z-direction. A unit vector is a vector whose length is 1. The right-handed orientation is summarized by
\mathbf i\times \mathbf j=\mathbf k.
Here \times denotes the cross product. The cross product itself is treated more fully later, but at this stage the formula is mainly an orientation convention. It fixes the positive z-direction once the positive x- and y-directions have been chosen. This matters later because signs in cross products, normal directions, surface orientation, and flux depend on orientation.
A point can also be represented by its position vector. The position vector of P=(x,y,z) is
\mathbf r=x\mathbf i+y\mathbf j+z\mathbf k.
Here \mathbf r is the vector from the origin O to the point P, and x, y, and z are its Cartesian components. A point and a position vector carry the same coordinate data, but they are conceptually different. A point is a location. A position vector is an arrow from the origin to that location. This distinction becomes important later when a moving particle is described by a time-dependent position vector \mathbf r(t).

The distance from the origin to P=(x,y,z) follows from the Pythagorean theorem. First project P onto the xy-plane. The projection is the point
Q=(x,y,0).
The distance from O=(0,0,0) to Q=(x,y,0) is
\sqrt{x^2+y^2}.
This is the ordinary two-dimensional distance formula in the xy-plane. The point P is then obtained from Q by moving vertically by z. Therefore the distance from O to P, denoted |\mathbf r|, is
|\mathbf r|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}.
Here |\mathbf r| means the length of the position vector \mathbf r. Geometrically, this formula says that the squared distance in space is the sum of the squared displacements in the three mutually perpendicular coordinate directions.
The same idea gives the distance between any two points. If
P_1=(x_1,y_1,z_1)
\quad\text{and}\quad
P_2=(x_2,y_2,z_2),
then the coordinate changes from P_1 to P_2 are
x_2-x_1,\qquad y_2-y_1,\qquad z_2-z_1.
The Euclidean distance between P_1 and P_2 is
d(P_1,P_2)=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2+(z_2-z_1)^2}.
Here d(P_1,P_2) denotes the straight-line distance from P_1 to P_2. The word Euclidean means that the distance is measured using ordinary straight-line geometry, so the Pythagorean theorem applies.
A useful way to understand the formula is that it turns a geometric question into an algebraic calculation. For example, suppose a triangle has vertices
A=(1,-1,2),\qquad B=(3,3,8),\qquad C=(2,0,1).
The squared side lengths are easier to compare than the side lengths themselves. We compute
|AC|^2=(2-1)^2+(0-(-1))^2+(1-2)^2=1+1+1=3,
|AB|^2=(3-1)^2+(3-(-1))^2+(8-2)^2=4+16+36=56,
and
|BC|^2=(2-3)^2+(0-3)^2+(1-8)^2=1+9+49=59.
Since
|AC|^2+|AB|^2=3+56=59=|BC|^2,
the triangle satisfies the Pythagorean relation with BC as the hypotenuse. Therefore the angle at A is a right angle. The important method is that right-angle questions can be answered by comparing squared distances.

The coordinate axes determine three coordinate planes. The xy-plane consists of all points whose z-coordinate is zero:
z=0.
The xz-plane consists of all points whose y-coordinate is zero:
y=0.
The yz-plane consists of all points whose x-coordinate is zero:
x=0.
These three planes divide three-dimensional space into eight regions called octants. The first octant is the region where all three coordinates are nonnegative:
x\geq 0,\qquad y\geq 0,\qquad z\geq 0.
This is the three-dimensional analogue of the first quadrant in the xy-plane. The reason there are eight octants is that each of the three coordinates may be positive or negative, giving 2^3=8 possible sign combinations.
Equations in x, y, and z describe sets of points in space. A single equation in three variables often describes a surface, although special cases may describe a curve, a point, or no points at all. For instance,
z=0
describes the xy-plane, and
z=-2
describes a horizontal plane two units below the xy-plane.
The equation
x+y+z=1
describes an oblique plane. It is called oblique because it is not parallel to any coordinate plane. It intersects the coordinate axes at
(1,0,0),\qquad (0,1,0),\qquad (0,0,1),
because setting two variables equal to zero determines the intercept on the remaining axis. The related equation
x+y+z=0
describes a parallel plane passing through the origin. Both equations have the same left-hand side, so they have the same orientation; changing the right-hand side shifts the plane.
A light bridge to the next geometry section is useful here. A plane is often written in the form
ax+by+cz=d.
Here a, b, c, and d are constants, while x, y, and z are the coordinates of a variable point on the plane. Later, the vector
a\mathbf i+b\mathbf j+c\mathbf k
will be interpreted as a normal vector to the plane, meaning a vector perpendicular to the plane. This normal-vector interpretation belongs more naturally to the later treatment of planes and vectors, but it explains why the coefficients a, b, and c matter geometrically.
A common source of confusion is that the same equation can describe different kinds of objects in different ambient spaces. In \mathbb R^2, the equation
x=y
describes a line in the plane. In \mathbb R^3, the same equation describes a plane, because z is unrestricted. Every point satisfying the equation has the form
(x,x,z),
where both x and z may vary freely. Two independent quantities are free, so the set is two-dimensional, not one-dimensional.



The equation
x^2+y^2=4
describes a circular cylinder of radius 2 whose axis is the z-axis. The reason is that the equation contains x and y, but not z. In every horizontal plane z=\text{constant}, the cross-section is the circle
x^2+y^2=4.
Because the same circle is repeated for every value of z, the surface extends parallel to the z-axis.
This example also shows the difference between a surface and a solid. The equation
x^2+y^2=4
describes only the cylindrical surface. The inequality
x^2+y^2\leq 4
