Indeed, answer C is correct. It should be exactly two and a half electron volts. It’s not that if you have more, the surplus of energy gets lost some way. You have to excite that exactly right to make an electron jump an orbit. It’s not that it can be more and then the excess gets dissipated in some way. That’s why you have discrete spectral lines in the absorption spectrum.
Okay, let’s have a 15-minute break here, and then we’ll continue with the laser and blackbody after.
So we’ll continue. Please take your seats.
There will now be two applications of absorption and emission-applications you’ve probably seen before. The laser, for sure, you’ve seen in secondary school. This is also nice. I will not go into too much detail. There is a follow-up course, Introduction to Photonics, in year two, actually this quarter, year two, that will make extensive use of the laser. I’m just showing the principle here.
So we’ve now established that atoms can interact with light by absorbing a photon, so going from a ground state to an excited state at a specific energy level. But it can also emit that same energy sometime later. It gets excited, and typically it wants to go back to its ground state. This may take some time, sometimes milliseconds, sometimes nanoseconds, but it wants to go back to the ground state.
If it emits this radiation, it goes in any direction: random direction, random phase, and emits this photon.
This can be amplified, and that’s called stimulated emission. If you shine light of a certain frequency-as photons at a certain frequency-on previously excited atoms, you can make these emit their photon. So one photon goes in, two photons come out, because you trigger this one into giving up its energy and sending out the photon. This then goes in the same direction with the same phase. This is called light amplification.
So you send one photon in, you get two out, because the atom was excited to a higher energy state exactly with that photon. Now you get coherent…
Page 8
…radiation from these atoms. If you do this a lot, you can make one coherent light beam. That’s called the laser.
Question? No, well, it has absorbed a photon already, and if you send a photon next to it, it will trigger this one into releasing the photon that it has absorbed already. So you send one in and then you get two out: the one you send in plus the one that was from the excited atom.
This is what’s done in the laser, which is an abbreviation for:
Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
Within a laser there is a tube with gas, and there’s continuous light reflecting back and forth in this tube. There’s a mirror that is 100% reflective on one side and a mirror that is slightly less reflective on the other side, so light can come out on that side.
Inside this tube, you want to achieve as many atoms in the excited level as possible. You want to have as many that can then go for stimulated emission. You do that by so-called population inversion. You invert, compared to the ground state, the number of atoms that are at the excited energy level, which is a metastable state that lasts around milliseconds.
By doing this, you can create a beam of very coherent and very in-phase light at a single frequency, so monochromatic light from this cooperative emission.
This is just an example of how this works.
A quick question then. Okay. Metastable means: if you excite an atom to a higher energy level, it tries to emit this photon already pretty soon, typically nanoseconds. A metastable state is a state in which it can stay a bit longer at that energy state. Think of milliseconds, which is long compared to nanoseconds.
This only works if you have atoms that are long enough in their excited state. Otherwise, you can’t trigger them into emitting that photon while triggering it. That’s why you need them longer at this excited state.
Yeah, in almost all cases it’s unstable if you excite an atom into a higher energy state. It wants to go back to a lower energy state. That’s what the force wants to do. That’s what gravity also wants to do: if you drop something, it wants to bring the gravitational energy down. A similar effect happens here.
So that’s how the laser works.
Another example is blackbody radiation, which relates to continuous spectra. This is at a very defined frequency: monochromatic light, so a very specific color of light. For blackbody radiation, we’re looking at continuous spectra.
What we’ve seen so far holds for gases; also in the laser, there’s a gas. If you have a continuous medium-fluid or solid-then you have a lot of atoms packed close together. Contrary to what you have in a gas, there the atoms do not interact. If one emits something, it doesn’t respond by causing others to react as well. In a continuous medium, there are a lot of interrelations between the atoms, a lot of reactions. As a result of that, you get not a single line, but a continuous spectrum of emissions.
It can also be the inverse. As we have gas that emits light at a certain frequency, that can also absorb light at a certain frequency. This is the absorption and emission spectra that I described earlier.
For an object that can emit a continuous spectrum, the inverse should also be true: it can absorb a continuous spectrum over a wide frequency range. That’s what’s called a blackbody.
A blackbody is an idealized case of a hot dense object that can absorb energy over a continuous spectrum. Think of a box that has absorbing insides. Light is shone through the box, and then it reflects, and with every bounce there is less light. Eventually it absorbs. If you look into your eye, also the center of your pupil looks black because no light is coming out. It also acts like a blackbody.
Similarly for emission, you can also have radiation. A blackbody is an idealized thing, just as a surface that has no friction, or a massless rope or pulley. This does not exist, but it’s nice to work with. You can make devices or boxes like this that mimic the effect of a blackbody.
For radiation, you probably noticed the Stefan-Boltzmann radiation law. The intensity of emitted radiation, total intensity, is a constant, the Boltzmann constant, times the temperature to the fourth, where temperature is in Kelvin. Don’t forget, or you’ll make a mistake.
So this is a radiation law. But the blackbody does not radiate at a single frequency, so the intensity has to result from…
Page 9
I’ll get back to my story in the next slide. I’ll get back to the intensity. Let me first give an example.
These are new slides, so I missed the flow a bit. An example of how this already can be observed is if you look at sunspots, or with sunglasses, please.
There’s an intensity ratio between hotter parts and less hot parts of the Sun. So there are these black spots on the Sun. They are not black in reality; it’s just that their intensity is much lower than what’s around them. Typically, or to give an example, the black spots, the cooler spots, are at 4,000 Kelvin, which is less hot than the rest of the Sun at 5,800 Kelvin.
So the intensity ratio is the difference in temperature to the fourth, because that relates to Boltzmann’s law. So that’s sigma (T^4). The ratio between the two-well, sigma drops out-so it’s just a temperature ratio to the fourth. So it’s a factor of 0.23, which is how much less these black spots radiate compared to the rest of the Sun.
On a picture with the proper filter, this looks like a darker spot on the Sun, but these are really cooler spots on the Sun caused by the vortices in the Sun, the magnetic fields there.
Okay, back to my story. Boltzmann’s law specifies total radiated intensity, but since this has to come from a continuous spectrum, there’s also a spectral emittance, as it’s called, which specifies what the intensity is per color, per wavelength. These curves look like this. Typically, they go to zero at low wavelength, which was quite a problem in the early 1910s and around that time, and the maximum scales with the temperature.
So there’s a Wien displacement law for blackbody radiation, which specifies where the maximum is:
[
\lambda_{\text{maximum}} \times T = \text{constant}
]
Again, temperature is in Kelvin. So this specifies that at a different temperature, you have a different maximum in wavelength. It describes where this curve is, and the total intensity follows from integrating all of this over the curve.
You can see that if it starts at zero here and it goes down to zero here, this integral will be finite. If you do that, you would find Boltzmann’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann’s law:
[
\sigma T^4
]
This sigma then relates to a lot of different constants.
There was a problem back in that day: they could not explain this. This is also new material compared to last year, and this also answers your question about the UV catastrophe.
Classical theory tried to predict this, and that was based on oscillators in a blackbody that could absorb light. If you tune these oscillators to have certain frequencies, you can cover the continuous spectrum. This was okay for higher wavelengths, but if you go to lower wavelengths, then the classical curve, Rayleigh’s curve, would explode. This goes like:
[
\frac{1}{\lambda^4}
]
So this would not go to zero if lambda approaches zero; this would explode. This was then called the ultraviolet catastrophe, because for lower wavelengths in the ultraviolet range you would have a catastrophe-a mathematical one-but that was what people were concerned about back then.
Planck solved this. He was the first one actually to define that this energy of these oscillators should be quantized, and that led him to derive:
[
E = hf
]
Then the energy states in which an oscillator could be would have to be integer multiples of this quantum of energy, (h) times (f), that scales with wavelength. But it can take only discrete values.
By doing that, he could derive a semi-empirical formula that did describe this behavior correctly. Later on, this was validated to be correct. Indeed, these energy levels have to be quantized in discrete steps. Einstein also confirmed this with the photoelectric effect, and that initiated the whole discussion on quantum physics.
So an example of this-and that’s probably also an example you’ll see next week in the guest lecture-is that you can look at colors of stars and see what temperatures they are.
Page 10
So I’ll confine myself to the visible spectrum here. There are lower-temperature stars that appear red, and higher-temperature stars that appear blue or violet. This relates to the temperature of the stars.
This shows the curves at three different temperatures: low-temperature stars. Well, this is the visible spectrum, so they have more red. If you have a higher-temperature star, that is shifted through the visible spectrum, but the balance within the visible spectrum is that there’s more violet or blue than the rest.
So that’s how this color can relate to the temperature of stars in the universe.
Yes. Yeah, this is-yes, the green is white stars here. I wouldn’t say uniform, but it covers the whole spectrum, biggest somewhat in the center, and then you would see it as white. So it would go from red to white to blue the hotter they get.
Just briefly, then try to write these concepts down in your own words: blackbody radiation and the laser. Then we’ll go to the core of, or the most difficult part of today as well: Schrödinger’s equation.
Okay, let’s now get to the exciting stuff. I can’t cover the rest of this lecture. There are three or four slides that I can also cover on Thursday, so I’ll see how far I get. This is me fine-tuning a bit the timing of the lecture. There will be plenty of time on Thursday anyway.
Schrödinger’s Equation
So the Schrödinger equation: how do we get there?
What we’ve seen before-where do we start from? We had Feynman’s interpretation. Light is a particle, light is a wave. It’s actually both or neither. Electrons also behave like particles or behave like waves. In reality, we just accept that they act like this, and we say they behave like neither. You could call it a particle wave, perhaps.
Have we given up an understanding? Well, I think we should come to terms with accepting that it is like this. But the good thing is that the quantum behavior of these atomic objects is similar for all of these small objects: photons, electrons, protons, neutrons. They all behave like this.
So once we can work with it, or have learned how to work with this, we can cover a large range of atomic particles. We could call these particle waves for lack of a better word, but actually we will use Schrödinger’s equation to derive a wave-like description for what happens.
What did Bohr say? This is a recap of a previous hour. Bound particles, so electrons that are connected in atoms, have quantized energy levels. They orbit the nucleus with quantized energy. They do not radiate if they are in the fixed orbits. They can make transitions between different orbits, and only then they absorb or emit.
This is a semi-classical model. We still used Newtonian mechanics to do these calculations. We looked at radial acceleration and Coulomb force. This works almost completely for the hydrogen atom, but not for many other atoms that have more electrons and more protons.
So we needed more, and that’s the step Bohr could not make, but Schrödinger did. We need to go to wave-like descriptions to describe what matter does, and that’s where Schrödinger’s equation comes in.
This is also a summary of last Thursday, when I talked about the two-slit experiment, and I’ll relate Schrödinger’s equation to this. There’s a difference in notation, however. Feynman used (\Phi), Schrödinger uses (\Psi), which is another Greek letter. It’s just a different way of writing.
So we have (\Phi), we have (\Psi). We will use (\Psi) in Schrödinger’s equation. It’s a matter of taste. Schrödinger is always using (\Psi). He also has (i) in there instead of (j) for the complex number, but that’s how physics works.
There’s a probability and a probability amplitude. I’ll relate Schrödinger’s equation to this, and the
Page 11
probability is the square of the probability amplitude. It’s slightly more intricate than this, but I’ll explain how that works in detail.
If you have an event that can occur in multiple ways, then you can sum the probability densities and then calculate probability. That’s what you’ve seen before. So I will not go into detail on this again; I covered this already.
What we’ll do is we start from here. We had Newtonian mechanics being inadequate to describe what happens in the photoelectric effect, X-ray production, and diffraction. We need to get to Schrödinger’s equation.
So how do we start? Let’s start 1D: one spatial dimension and time. We need something that is wave-like, so this will have to relate to the wave equation that we’ve seen before in Module 5. We know that we have Planck’s law, which defines the energy of photons, and de Broglie’s hypothesis that relates momentum. But that describes momentum of photons.
So these are boundary conditions that we have to satisfy.
As a brief recap, what was a wave equation again? That was this scary-looking thing with partial differentials in here:
[
\frac{\partial^2 y(x,t)}{\partial x^2}
\frac{1}{v^2}
\frac{\partial^2 y(x,t)}{\partial t^2}
]
Twice the spatial derivative of the wave (y) as a function of (x) and (t) equals (1/v^2) times twice the time derivative of that same function.
The solutions were traveling waves. So we had solutions that look like (y(x,t)), being combinations of sines and cosines of a very specific argument. A forward-traveling wave would be:
[
kx - \omega t
]
Then you can have a ratio between (a) and (b) to describe an arbitrary wave. The wave number relates to (\omega / v). That’s important here, and there’s a wavelength that relates to (v/f). So this is how the wave equation works.
Put that into the wave equation. We get twice the spatial derivative, twice the temporal derivative, and these terms in the curly braces are the same, so we can get rid of those. This gives the dispersion relation:
[
k^2 = \frac{\omega^2}{v^2}
]
So we have:
[
k = \pm \frac{\omega}{v}
]
Let’s now try the same approach for particle waves. What I would like you to do is just follow the derivation. I will not ask this derivation at an exam; that is way too extensive. If you can follow why we get to the Schrödinger equation, and I’ll show you how, then what we do next is work with the Schrödinger equation. But I think showing how we get there will help you understand why it has that form.
So let’s start with a particle that is free. There are no forces on it. The particle experiences no force, so it has to be at a constant potential energy. We’ll work that in later. For now, it has no potential energy, and then the energy has to equal the kinetic energy of the particle:
[
E = \frac{1}{2}mv^2
]
We can also write this in terms of the momentum:
[
E = \frac{p^2}{2m}
]
So that’s a momentum that I used to write the kinetic energy.
I also know that we have Planck’s equation, which specifies the energy of such a free particle, a quantum particle:
[
E = hf = \hbar \omega
]
If we divide by (2\pi) and multiply by (2\pi), (2\pi f = \omega), and (h / 2\pi = \hbar), right? So the energy is also (\hbar \omega), and these have to be equal because that describes the energy of the particle.
On top of that, we have a relation for the momentum, de Broglie’s momentum relation:
[
p = \frac{h}{\lambda} = \hbar k
]
Again, here you see it written out:
[
k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}
]
and
[
\frac{h}{2\pi} = \hbar
]
So let’s equate this kinetic energy to the Planck energy of the particle. If we write (p) in terms of (\hbar k), we get:
[
\frac{\hbar^2 k^2}{2m} = \hbar \omega
]
So I get this equation that has to hold. This is similar to what we had for the wave equation. For the classical wave equation, we had this dispersion relation. For quantum mechanics, we have this dispersion
Page 12
relation. It still relates (k) to (\omega) in some way. That’s what the wave equation does, but it’s also different.
There’s (k^2) and (\omega^2) here. There’s (k^2) and (\omega), so the scaling is off, and that makes Schrödinger’s equation a different type of wave equation.
For quantum mechanics, we have:
[
\omega \propto k^2
]
and for the string we have:
[
\omega \propto k
]
So that’s the difference already that we’ve identified.
How do we solve this? Let’s introduce a wave function, and we’ll start building from there. Let’s use a wave function, capital psi, of (x) and (t):
[
\Psi(x,t)
]
There’s a spatial dimension (x)-we do a 1D case here-and time (t). Let’s have this wave function describe the state of a particle. This wave function should contain all the information we need to describe where the particle is, how the particle behaves, etc.
Let’s assume that, since we’re talking waves, it should have some harmonic behavior. Similar to what we have for the particle moving on a string, the wave on the string, let’s do:
[
kx - \omega t
]
also here, for a particle of mass (m), a defined momentum, and a defined energy, in line with what we know from de Broglie and Planck. Let’s assume this form and see how we get to the wave equation.
If it has this form, if we differentiate with respect to (x), we get (k) in front. We get a factor (k). If you differentiate with respect to time, we get the factor (-\omega), to be correct.
Spatial differentiation gives (k); time differentiation gives (\omega). What we had previously is we had a (k^2) on one side and an (\omega) on the other side. So we should do twice spatial differentiation on the left-hand side, and one time differentiation on the right-hand side, to get to this (k^2) here and (\omega) on that side.
I’ll let that sink in a bit. This is different from the wave equation we’ve seen before. There, we had twice time differentiation on the right-hand side. That’s why:
[
\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2}
]
So let’s do the spatial derivative. Twice the spatial derivative of the expression we assumed gives us (-k^2) in front. So we need not (k^2), but this factor:
[
\frac{\hbar^2 k^2}{2m}
]
If we multiply by minus some constants:
[
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}
]
we get to the expression we want.
So the left-hand side is pretty easy. Twice spatial differentiation gives us a factor (-k^2), and then we multiply by this factor to get to this expression. So what I know already is that the left-hand side of Schrödinger’s equation should be like:
[
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}
\frac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial x^2}
]
That should be the left-hand side, because that will exactly give me this expression that I need on the left-hand side.
The right-hand side needs to yield:
[
\hbar \omega \Psi
]
So how do we do that? Let’s try to get to this factor (\omega). Let’s do:
[
C\hbar
]
times the first time derivative. Bear in mind we need one (\omega), so we need to do one time differentiation. Let’s try this and then find what (C) needs to be in terms of (A) and (B).
Okay, so let’s try this and put in the solution of (\Psi) that we assumed. Now, if we take time derivatives, the left-hand side we’ve done already. The right-hand side gets (-\omega) times minus sine, so that’s (\omega) times sine, and then we have minus (\omega) times sine becomes cosine, so minus (B).
Page 13
cosine of that argument, and then we see that.
Okay, this does not make sense yet. Let’s try to make sense of it.
So we do get the factor ℏω and ℏ^2k^2 / 2m, which was the factor we needed to get. So we want this to be equal. So this on the right-hand side cancels against that on the left-hand side if we want that factor to hold. And then we find this expression:
A cos + B sin = C A sin - C B cos
So this can only hold if:

A = -C B
B = C A

Only then do we get a valid solution, right? Since the amplitudes in front of the sine have to be equal, and the amplitudes in front of the cosine have to be equal, only then this holds.
So we get:

A = -C B
B = C A

And if we substitute B into here, we get:
A = -C^2 A
So:
C^2 = -1
So then C should be the square root of minus one, so plus or minus i. Convention is to choose i here, C being the imaginary number.
It’s not nice that we got complex numbers, but sorry. What? Your seven is not for you then?
So what we then get is: if C = i, then B = i A. So we can put that in the solution we have. But this solution basically has B = i A. So the solution becomes an amplitude times:
cos(argument) + i sin(argument)
So that’s then the complex wave that we get as a solution for Schrödinger’s equation, basically.
So to summarize the results in this: we found that this needs to be:
iℏ ∂ψ / ∂t
with C here being the imaginary number.
So the left-hand side we’ve seen, the right-hand side we’ve now seen. Then we get to Schrödinger’s equation here. Sorry, the ω needs to go. Yeah, this came from differentiation. Correct that. So:
iℏ ∂ψ / ∂t
So this is a wave function, but a special one, because it has complex solutions. Well, Schrödinger established this, and the solution in general form can be written as:
A [cos(argument) + i sin(argument)]
Well, this is something you’ve seen before using Euler. You can write this as a complex exponential. So the solutions are complex exponentials. They are a solution for the Schrödinger equation.
Okay, this was a lot. Try to summarize this for yourselves. Think of this as a wave equation, but a special one, and then I’ll show how to work with this. I understand this is a lot to take in, and Schrödinger’s equation - that’s probably the first time you see it when you see it derived.
Let’s try to interpret. Let’s try to make a bit of sense of what this means. So this is what I showed before: we have the Schrödinger equation plus a solution, which are complex exponentials. But it does contain the imaginary number i, so it’s always i here, not j.
So this means that wave functions are always complex functions. But the world around us is real-valued. We see things as they are, not on a complex plane. It’s real-valued. How is that possible?
Well, let me talk you through some examples. If you have a free particle that has a definite momentum ℏk and an energy, then the wave function at time zero is this. So it extends all over space. cos(kx) has values everywhere for the whole x range. So we don’t know where the particle is. It extends from minus infinity to plus infinity.
This is the real and imaginary part. So in this case - well, in any case, in general - we can write the wave function as: we can separate the exponential with the time behavior and the spatial behavior. It extends over all of space. That’s very inconvenient if you talk about where to find a particle.
So let’s specify this a bit clearer. The wave function describes the state of a particle, and these are definitions in the following way. The absolute value squared is the probability density function of a particle.
This is the chance of finding the particle at a position. No, it describes the density of finding a particle at a position. If you want to calculate the chance of finding a particle at, say, a small interval on x, you define x and x + Δx, so a small interval on the x axis. Then this is the chance of finding that particle there at time t.
And we have to bear in mind that ψ is complex. So the absolute value squared is the real part squared plus the imaginary part squared. So that’s what you have to keep in mind when doing these calculations.
Page 14
So let’s have two slides on probability.
Probability P on an event is always ranging from 0 to 1. If it’s 0, it’s not possible; if it’s 1, it’s certain.
The chance of finding a particle at a position less than x_1 follows from an integral over the probability density function up to that point. So from minus infinity to x_1 is the chance of finding a particle at position x_1.
Depending on the shape of the probability density function, it’s likely or not likely to find it. We also know that the probability of finding the particle everywhere should be one, because the particle has to be somewhere. So if I would integrate from minus infinity to plus infinity, I would get one. This is called normalization, and this is in line with the probability of finding the particle anywhere being one.
Okay, if you have a free particle - so for the sine and the cosine that extend infinitely - well, you can’t integrate that. It’s not possible to normalize that, because the value of that integral would be infinite. You can’t normalize that, so we have to solve this in some way. I’ll get back to that in the next slide.
I think I’ll need two more minutes to do this. Well, let’s make it three after this slide.
The expected position of a particle - to find that somewhere - is x times the probability density, and we integrate this from minus infinity to infinity. Then we find the expected position of a particle, and that would be the expected outcome if you would do a measurement on the location of the particle.
There is also uncertainty in a position, and that relates to the variance of x. That is then x^2 times this probability density function and the same integral minus the expectation. So actually it’s this one, sorry:
(x - average value)^2
And you could rewrite this into mathematics that involve just ψ and e, and the standard deviation is then the square root of the variance.
Well, these are definitions. What matters mainly is this slide: that you know that you can find the particle at a certain position, and you use a probability density function - the square of that - to do that.
To give some examples: a single traveling wave is not localized. That was the example I gave. But if you have a sum of traveling waves, you can generate a pulse shape like this, and this pulse shape has a defined length in the x direction.
So this is not extending to infinity. It’s zero here and zero here, and this gives a certain behavior for the real and imaginary part. You find a particle within this range. It’s expected that you find a particle within this range.
And you do this by writing this as a wave pulse. By doing that, you get an average wave number and an average wavelength of the particle, which is kind of a superposition of all kinds of waves. But still, you can define an average wave number, because you have a range of wave numbers that apply. And that means that there is a certain wavelength and a certain region in space where you can find the particle.
Oh, sorry. So to set up such a wave, for every wave number you can give a certain amplitude, and this works like a Fourier series for a particle. Well, an amplitude spread over wave number. And if you would calculate the probability density for this pulse shape, you would find a probability density like this.
So there’s a certain width Δx. It’s practically zero outside this range, and the chance is highest of finding the particle at this position - x is zero in this case - where it has its maximum.
Page 15
This ball still has the aspects of both a particle and a wave. So there’s a chance that you find the particle at the position where it’s highest, but there’s a wave-like description that analyzes this, because it really is determined by this wave function. So that’s why it acts both like particle and wave, and that’s how the solutions to the Schrödinger equation work.
So in a particle sense, there is localization in space. There’s a finite Δx over which this has values. But in a wave sense, it still has a periodic structure, because it’s built from these contributions over different frequencies. This is called a wave packet. I’ll get back to this topic on Thursday again.
So the last slides: yeah. There’s also uncertainty involved. If you have a narrow function in k space, or for every wave number you know what the amplitude is, you will get a broad pulse in the solution space, or vice versa: if you have a broad function, a broad pulse in k space.
So these relate to the wavelengths and the amplitude at that wavelength. If you have a broader pulse, you would have a smaller pulse in the spatial domain. This is exactly how a Fourier integral works. This is a property of Fourier integrals.
If you have a very narrow pulse and you calculate the Fourier response of that, you get a broad spectrum. If you have a very broad pulse, you would get a narrower spectrum. A broad pulse in the time domain gives a narrower spectrum in the k domain.
I’ll get back to this on Thursday more in detail, and I’ll do this on Thursday as well. So this is indeed four slides too many to cover here.
So what we did today - and there will be the studio classroom after, also with the explanation of the Metron test and some questions on module 7 - we looked at:

the Bohr model of the atom,
the laser,
black-body radiation,
how to derive Schrödinger’s equation for a 1D particle,
and a bit of interpreting this.

I’ll get back to this on Thursday. So please stay around for the pseudo classroom, and let’s start in 15 minutes. Let’s start 10 to 11.

physics-for-ee/sources/986217-english-1.content:
Summary
This lecture chunk explains quantum entanglement using the analogy of Professor Bertlmann’s mismatched socks. Classical deterministic socks have definite colors before observation, are locally determined, and merely reveal preexisting correlations when measured. Quantum socks, by contrast, represent entangled quantum objects whose individual properties are indefinite before measurement, become definite only upon measurement, and show correlations that appear instantaneously across distance without transmitting usable information faster than light. The lecture introduces the hidden-variable debate and John Stewart Bell’s correlation experiment, where violations of Bell’s inequality support quantum entanglement over local hidden-variable explanations. It also connects entanglement to wave function collapse, photon polarization experiments, electron spin pairs with net zero spin, and quantum computing with qubits in superpositions of multiple states. The final page summarizes the larger lecture sequence on wave functions, the one-dimensional Schrödinger equation, finite square wells, quantum oscillators, tunneling, and entanglement.

Yeah, there was a question. Why? Well inside the barrier there’s, that’s due to mathematics. So if you recall for the finite square well, there’s these exponential functions that are solutions to the differential equation. Also inside the barrier there is this energy that makes that only exponential solutions are valid solutions in for the Schrodinger equation. This is relative to the potential here.
So if this is almost zero, then this picture still holds conceptually. Come again, I’m not following completely.
Page 9
Let’s discuss afterwards.
This is okay. My main point here is that instead of a potential well, you can also have a potential barrier, which is an energy barrier that the particle may or may not overcome. If you think quantum mechanically, then the particle may overcome this barrier, and there is a chance you find it outside.
So there is a certain tunneling chance, and you can imagine that if the barrier is wider or higher, then this exponential decays quicker, and there is less chance of finding the particle outside.
Is there decay before the barrier? I know there is. This is due to boundary conditions. The solution has to be continuous across the barrier, and if it goes exponentially here, then it has to connect to that from the outside. You need a solution that is continuous in space, because that is a property of a wave equation: that you find continuous solutions.
Yep, that relates to that.
So examples of tunneling, applications of tunneling, are well transistors, Josephson junctions, nuclear fusion, and tunnel diodes. All of this relates to tunneling. The scanning tunneling microscope, for instance, is a microscope that creates images at the atomic scale, and it is based on electrons tunneling through this small distance between the specimen that you are measuring and the probe. It catches electrons that tunnel through this layer. You bring that really, really close to the surface, around one nanometer, and by measuring these electrons you see where there is locally a profile on the specimen. So that is a way to make a height profile of a specimen.
Got pictures like this, for instance. This is color-coded not because you measure color; you measure the intensity of electrons, for instance. So this is how you can do that.
There are other applications. Recall when we had Rutherford’s experiment with the alpha particles shot at a gold sheet. The alpha particle itself comes from the decay of a radium atom, and then it emits a helium nucleus. Basically, that is an alpha particle. Suppose that this is a radium nucleus, and then the alpha particle needs to get out. That alpha particle needs to overcome a certain energy to get out. If it has a certain energy, it can tunnel through that barrier. So it is locally confined here.
But if you are outside, there is the 1/r dependence of the electric potential. This is not a square barrier, but an exponentially decaying barrier, and still there is a chance of finding the alpha particle outside. This is how it can tunnel through the barrier and escape the radium atom.
So briefly write down what tunneling means and how it can be used. Again, if you understand the concept, that is fine. That is enough for this course.
So one last topic before we go to some lighter material: that is the harmonic oscillator. That is similar to what you see in Module 5, simple harmonic motion, but now in a quantum sense. It is similar, but not quite.
Let’s look at a simple mass-spring system where there is a restoring force:
F = -k' x
I have used prime here because we have k already for wave number. So let k' denote the spring constant, in newtons per meter, and k the wave number, in one per meter. This is k'. I hope I did not make any writing mistakes. These are new slides, but if so, I will correct them.
We have this differential equation for the simple harmonic motion. You will recall that, hopefully, and you can define a natural frequency:
ω = sqrt(k' / m)
This also relates to a potential energy for the system:
U = 1/2 k' x^2
which is a quadratic function, zero in the middle. That is how this works.
If you think classically, if a particle has a certain energy level E, then it can oscillate between -a and a, but not further. That is the range over which the amplitude spans. In Newtonian mechanics, this is restricted to that range, but in quantum mechanics, of course, there is a catch: you can find the particle outside.
There is a possibility that you have an amplitude less than -a or larger than +a, and I will show you why that is and what these functions look like.
Page 10
So if an object oscillates with a certain frequency, an angular frequency ω - think of an electron going around an atom, around a nucleus, sorry - then this would emit electromagnetic radiation at that frequency. So the energy that the particle has should relate somehow to the frequency that the particle has.
The energy levels are:
E = hf
which can be written as:
E = ℏω
For ω, we can express that in terms of the oscillator that we had:
ω = sqrt(k' / m)
Let’s try to put this in Schrödinger’s equation. But now, instead of the potential being just a value, a barrier, or a well, we now have a potential energy function, this spring-like restoring force:
U(x) = 1/2 k' x^2
So we put that where the U was previously. Solutions to this would be solutions that satisfy what a quantum harmonic oscillator looks like.
For such a differential equation, we always need boundary conditions. We need that the wave function goes to zero as x tends to infinity. So it should not be everywhere in space if there is a potential acting on a particle, but it can extend beyond the classical notion of energy. It should go to zero as x goes to infinity.
Yes, sorry. No, it could only be verified experimentally that this way of implementing a potential is a correct way of doing that in Schrödinger’s equation. So a U(x) term in front of ψ(x) is the correct way of including potential energy. This can be many energies in 3D. This will be covered in a later slide. This will be a Hamiltonian operator acting on the wave function. I will get back to what that means in a few later slides. That is the easy part, which I will just sketch how this works.
Okay, so we want to find solutions for Schrödinger’s equation, the time-independent Schrödinger equation, with this potential energy. We have these boundary conditions. The wave function has to go to zero if x goes to infinity.
By doing that - and now the book even does not clearly contain the derivation - the result is that there are defined energy levels at which this can take place. Also, the steps between these energy levels would correspond to an energy transition for a particle oscillating, and that then relates to the energy that is ℏ times ω.
So what you find here is that you have:
Eₙ = (n + 1/2) ℏω
as the allowable energy levels for a harmonic oscillator, for a quantum harmonic oscillator. The lowest one is n = 0, so we have:
E_0 = 1/2 ℏω
Then you go up in steps of ℏω for the next energy levels, and all of these are admissible energy levels for the particle. If you know it has a certain energy, then a wave function belongs to that, and it has a chance of finding the particle outside this classical range of these amplitudes.
You could even find it here and here. So that is what quantum mechanically happens.
So there is a ground energy level at n = 0. The energy cannot be zero, but the lowest energy state can happen at n = 0. You could also start at n = 1 and then put -1/2; it is just a definition.
Go ahead.
Yes, I will get back to these in the next slides. I will show the wave functions.
Why is there 1/2?
Yeah, this really relates to the mathematics that follows from the boundary conditions. This is not derived in the book, and I have no clue how to derive that myself. I am just stating how it is. I can show the wave functions, and if you know what these look like, that is sufficient for this course.
Yeah, and there are infinitely many energy levels, each separated by ℏω.
That is also a property here. For every energy level, say E_3 here, there is a maximum amplitude +a and -a if you think of a classical oscillator, a Newtonian oscillator. It cannot extend beyond that amplitude. Quantum mechanically, it can.
Page 11
So what do these look like? The n = 0 energy level looks like this.
Again, exponential tails outside the classical range. It goes from -a to a. Classically, you would find the particle here. Classically, the probability density would look like this curve. The probability density of a sine is like a bathtub curve. It oscillates, and there is a higher probability of finding it at the far ends because there is lower velocity there.
But the quantum mechanical one looks really different. It has a single maximum, so it is most likely to find it in the middle, whereas that is different from the classical oscillator. It has these exponential tails. If you go to higher modes, then this starts to look a bit like the blue curve, but still not quite. There are always these exponential tails of finding the particle outside this amplitude range that is allowed classically.
Yeah, so x larger than a is possible.
How does n relate to a? For a higher energy level, you would go up in the curve here. For a higher energy level, you would get a higher amplitude for the oscillation, because that would happen between this value on the x-axis and this value. So a scales with the number.
No, it is like this parabola. That is why, for higher n, you find a higher range for the amplitudes. That is also why this -a over a range increases with the number. That is why the blue curves change. It is not a constant one. You have more energy, so a larger amplitude that can vibrate between classically.
These are called Hermite functions in mathematics. They are not covered in this course or in the book. That is advanced mathematics courses. But mathematicians like these and can work with these.
What is important here is that, especially for the lowest mode, there is really a different probability for the classical one, confined from -a to +a, and the quantum mechanical one, which has the highest chance of finding it in the middle and again these exponential tails.
So these are three cases in which we try to apply Schrödinger’s equation in 1D with a potential term to two applications. I have the square wave potential, or the square well potential; tunnelling, which I covered only conceptually; and then the oscillator, which I could link to Module 5, where it is really different from the question so far.
It may take a while to wrap your head around this. Starting now, try to write this concept down on why it is different, for instance. Try to formulate that in your own words: why the quantum mechanical oscillator is different from a Newtonian oscillator.
To sketch what would be next: this is covered in the book, not part of the course. If you would extend this to 3D cases, then the math explodes. That is not what we are going to do. If you understand the concepts in 1D, that is fine.
If you have a particle that is moving at a velocity that is much lower than light speed, so non-relativistically, you can have Schrödinger’s equation in 3D. Instead of just having an x coordinate, you now have a position vector x, y, z. The time behavior with iℏ is still the same. On the right-hand side, everything is now captured in a Hamiltonian operator, which contains all the energy-type functions, all the spatial wave behavior, etc.
This operator contains all forms of energy: kinetic energy, potential energy, spin, if you think about 3D objects. All of that is confined into this operator, which I am not going to bother writing out.
Still, solutions you could display in a similar way as we have done before. For 1D, you have one quantum number. It makes sense that for a 3D particle in a 3D box, there are three quantum numbers that describe the different orthogonal directions x, y, z in which the particle can be.
Then, instead of just the principal quantum number, there are two more now. You have three numbers to indicate every state of the particle, and there are many, many more states. You can have many versions of the n = 2 state, for instance, and there is one n = 1 state. For every higher state, there are many more permutations of states, basically, of geometry that are permitted.
Page 12
So there is a principal, or main, quantum number that relates to the energy. Then there is one that relates to angular momentum, and one that relates to the orientation of the angular momentum, so it is a magnetic quantum number. But the energy levels are still similar to what Bohr derived for the hydrogen atom, for sure.
Then you get all kinds of different configurations. Let me see. This is the n = 2 state, I think. There are angular momenta. Instead of just rotating around the axis, you can have one that precesses like this, one at a higher angle θ. That is not what we are going to do. You will learn about spherical coordinates in Math 2 next quarter.
But still, there we do not relate that to quantum mechanics. This is just to sketch what is in the field. For each n, there are n^2 energy levels that have the same energy, the same fundamental energy. So we have permutations of these energies.
What does this look like then? Instead of a sine wave that describes where the particle is, a spatial sine wave, you now have fuzzy clouds, basically, that describe the radial behavior of where to find the particle. The intensity here is now the probability. So the bluer it is, the higher the probability of finding it there.
There is the n = 1 state, the n = 2 state, where there are two local maxima. There is a lower chance of finding it in this shell around the origin. Think of this as a spherical well, a cross-section of a sphere in which you can find the particle, and similarly for higher orders. There are pictures in the book that also have the angular version of this. This is just to sketch the main idea.
Are there questions on this? Please focus on the content of this course, not this part. This is really advanced stuff which is not covered in the standard curriculum. There are electives on this, of course, but please only do that if you pass your first year and if you are interested.
Okay, now the last topic, which is quantum entanglement, one of the fundamental principles of quantum computing. This is what Einstein called spooky action at a distance.
Entanglement is when multiple objects - say you have a pair of electrons or a pair of photons - share a single quantum state. An electron can be an up spin or down spin. If you have a pair of electrons, then this belongs together: one of them is an up spin, one of them is a down spin. You do not know which one is which until you make a measurement. I will get back to what that means in a second.
There was a paper in 1935 by Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen, the EPR paper, that showed some anxiety about this. Especially Einstein was really concerned about the lack of locality. He was not happy that there are no hidden variables that describe what is happening. He called this “spooky action at a distance,” and until his death he could not agree with this concept, that this was really how it happened.
But it was later proven by John Stuart Bell that it really happens like that. I will get back to that in detail.
So what they proposed at that time was: okay, this cannot be true. There have to be hidden variables that we have not been able to measure yet. There are hidden variables that describe what is happening exactly.
John Stuart Bell had a very nice story on this, and this worked up to Bell’s theorem. He explained this with a very nice story. I have linked the story. It is a nice read on the IEEE Spectrum, and this is also what the slides are based on. This is about Professor Bertlmann.
He is a professor who wears two different types of socks. I have to do this and stop; you understand, right? He wears two different types of socks. He always wears mismatched socks. If you know that one sock is pink, the other one has to be blue, and that is what Alice and Bob also know. So he wears
Page 13
If his left sock is pink, the other one is not pink for sure. So they decide to spy on his socks. If Alice sees a blue sock, then instantaneously Bob knows that the color of the other sock has to be pink, or the other way around. They know that these are deterministic socks. I’ll get back to what that means.
Also, the socks are correlated: he always wears a pair that has two different colors. So once you know that one sock is blue, the other one has to be pink. They are real; they have a color. Even without making a measurement, you know that one is blue and one is pink; you just don’t know which one. It is probably deterministic: on even days in the week he wears the pink one right and the blue one left, etc. So there is no randomness involved. They are local, so they only depend on nearby surroundings. They are stacked like that in his closet.
So he puts on one pair every day of these mismatched socks. Then Professor Bertlmann tries to screw Bob and Alice over: he wears quantum socks. This means that the socks are entangled. You don’t know what color the socks have until you make a measurement. If Alice then measures one of the socks, then instantaneously she knows that the other sock needs to be the other color. That’s how entanglement works. They are connected, but only when she measures one sock. Then you also know the color of the other sock. Before the measurement, you don’t know which sock has which color. That’s an important fact here.
So if she measures the pink sock, then the other one has to be blue. If she measures a blue sock, then the other one has to be pink. So these are quantum socks.
They have special properties. They are not real. They’re unreal. They don’t have a color before you measure them. So you don’t know what the color is; only when you measure do you know the color. They are non-deterministic. So there’s a 50% chance of finding a pink sock and 50% chance of finding a blue sock. This is not determined by something that is hidden underneath. That’s the hidden variable part here.
They are non-local, which means that they are not in pairs. Well, they are in pairs, a quantum pair, but it is not that what Bob sees depends on what Alice measures, or the other way around. Only then do you know what the color of the sock is. So one depends on the other. That is what non-local means in this sense.
Yeah, that’s one of the debates that Einstein had. The instantaneousness of it still happens. You may think that you are then conveying information faster than the speed of light because it is instantaneous, but there is no information yet because you don’t know beforehand what the color of the sock is. That would be information if you knew that you would measure a pink sock and then the other one would be blue. Then you’re transferring information. But you don’t know yet what the color is, and that’s why you don’t transfer information yet. So information does not transfer faster than the speed of light.
What propagates at the speed of light? So not instantaneous. Yeah, say you have two different color photons that are entangled. Then if you measure one, the other one updates instantly. That is still what happens, and that’s the weird thing about this. I’ll get back to what that means in the next slides.
Even if the socks are far apart, this still happens. So Professor Bertlmann: if you send one sock into space and the other one in a different direction into space, and you look at them through telescopes, if you measure one to be pink, then the other one is blue. That’s the entangled part: instantaneously measure this one, the other one is blue, and vice versa. Measure this one to be blue, the other one is pink instantaneously, even if they’re far apart.
So what puzzled the scientists was:
Page 14
How come they always choose different colors if you look at them? If you have one to be pink, the other one is not pink. Why is that? Does the one sock know when the measurement on the second sock has been done? Does the second sock know when the measurement on the first sock has been done? They were really puzzled about this.
So what they thought was that there is a hidden variable at play that would determine what would come out of the measurement. Then it would only seem that you instantaneously update what happens to the other sock.
John Stuart Bell devised a correlation experiment for this. If this hidden variable theory is correct, then entanglement is just an illusion. It’s not true. There’s something at play that determines what color the socks have. If it’s incorrect, if there are no hidden variable theories that can explain this, then entanglement really links the socks, and they are entangled as I just explained: if you measure one, the other gets updated instantaneously.
Well, I don’t get the first word. What is that, the color? Or this could be an up spin or a down spin of an electron. I mean, I like the socks example because John Stuart Bell wrote the story about this. No, no, no, I’ll get back to what this means in practice in a few slides. And if the question pertains after that, I’ll try to answer it better.
What they found experimentally was that there was no difference between these spooky socks-spooky action at a distance-and the hidden variable socks. It really works like this. Bell devised an experiment to distinguish between these situations. He devised an inequality. The sum of several probabilities had to be less than two to have entanglement not be true. But if you then do a correlation measurement and find a value larger than two, then entanglement is the only possible explanation of that experiment. In the meanwhile, there have been numerous experiments confirming that these quantum correlations really exceed Bell’s inequality. So really, entanglement plays a role.
This is really the essence of quantum mechanics: once you do a measurement on one thing, you influence something else, even if the objects are entangled. What that means for the socks, I’ll get back to; how the socks relate to other more realistic examples. Socks are not quantum objects, of course.
Before you do the measurement, there was really no red color sock and a left color sock. They were really indefinite; they were not defined yet. They were a single quantum object that had two states: pink or blue. It’s getting annoying now.
So this is really the essence of quantum mechanics. I’ve linked to this article again and some very nice Fermilab YouTube videos. There’s also a very nice quantum experiment in which you have a polarizer filter like this and a polarizing filter like that, which means that no light is coming through. If you would insert a polarizing filter at a 45-degree angle in between, then light would come through. So it’s really mind-blowing that it works like that. Photons still get through, and that’s something that quantum mechanics only can explain-well, can describe; I wouldn’t say explain.
So entanglement is really a property of a quantum system that describes how much, or the amount by which, multiple objects share a single state. Only when you do a measurement do you disentangle them. That’s sometimes what you hear: you have a superposition of two wave functions. When you do a measurement, the wave function collapses to one of the two solutions. Wave function collapse is what that’s called.
This is also at the heart of quantum computing. The qubits in quantum computing use this entanglement between electron spins. That means that the computer memory is in a superposition of multiple states simultaneously, and this allows certain calculations to become quicker, or very much quicker. Only certain calculations benefit from this, so I will not go into detail about this. There’s a whole DIFFER institute on the TU/e campus that is:
Page 15
Really looking into this. There’s a master’s part in electrical engineering that is focusing on quantum computing. This is just to give you a grasp of the complexity that is involved there.
To get back to a more realistic example, you can think of two electrons that originate from the same atom. I think the spin of an atom has to be zero, so the net spin has to be zero. So if one is an up spin, one is a down spin, or the other way around. You don’t know which of the states it is.
Suppose you label the electrons one and two. One of them would be an up spin, the other then a down spin, or vice versa: down spin, up spin. This is an entangled pair. Only when you do a measurement on the electrons do you know that one is in up spin. If afterwards you would do a measurement on particle two, on the second electron, that would always be in down spin. So that’s how these are entangled.
Similarly, if you measure the first electron to have a down spin, the second one will always have an up spin. So it might be a nice experiment for the final test that I make entangled pairs of students: one of them fails the exam, one of them passes the exam, and I didn’t do the measurement just by rolling the dice. Who’s in favor? No, let’s not do that. But this is how entanglement works.
Right. So this also concludes the lecture. There are two more slides, this one and the next one. I hope I gave you a glimpse of what wave functions mean and how they can be used. We looked at solutions to the 1D Schrödinger equation, especially the time-independent version, where you can look at the spatial part only, which has these weird exponential tails. The finite square well, we did the quantum oscillator, we looked at tunneling and entanglement.
With that, I would like to thank you for attending, for your attention. I enjoyed teaching this course a lot, and I wish you good luck with the exam. Thank you for staying here. People are really here from start to end. Thank you for that, and good luck. I’ll see you next Monday actually, but already good luck with the exam.

signals-and-systems/aliasing-problem-sol.content:
Aliasing Problem Solving with Multiple Sinusoids
Source: Signals and Systems Full Notes: Sinusoids, Spectra, Sampling, Aliasing, and FIR Filters
Locations: Page 25
The notes solve for an unknown sinusoidal frequency by using aliasing and phasor addition after sampling. The given signal is x(t)=4\cos(2\pi32t-\pi/6)+7\cos(2\pi f_2t-\pi/2) with 32<f_2<200, sampled at f_s=160 Hz, and the observed discrete-time signal is x[n]=3\cos(2\pi n/5+\pi/2). The known 32 Hz component maps to \tilde{\omega}_1=2\pi(32/160)=2\pi/5. signals-and-systems/block-diagram-reduct.title: Block Diagram Reduction Rules
signals-and-systems/block-diagram-reduct.content:
Block Diagram Reduction Rules
Source: Signals and Systems Full Notes: Sinusoids, Spectra, Sampling, Aliasing, and FIR Filters
Locations: Page 99
Block diagram reduction uses algebraic transformations that preserve signal relationships while rearranging takeoff points and summing junctions into forms that are easier to solve. Page 99 emphasizes that when a signal departs from a point, the takeoff point can be moved across a block if a compensating block is inserted. If a takeoff originally before G(s) is moved after G(s) but must still represent the original input U(s), the branch must include 1/G(s). Conversely, if an output takeoff after G(s) is moved before the block but must still represent Y(s), the branch must include G(s). Summing junctions can also be moved across blocks. Moving a summing junction ahead of a block requires multiplying each input branch by G(s); moving it behind the block requires dividing the bypassed input by G(s). These rules allow complex diagrams to be reduced through series, parallel, and feedback equivalents.

Moving a takeoff point across a block requires compensating by G(s) or 1/G(s).

signals-and-systems/cascaded-discrete-ti.content:
Cascaded Discrete-Time LTI Systems
Source: Signals and Systems Full Notes: Sinusoids, Spectra, Sampling, Aliasing, and FIR Filters
Locations: Page 41, Page 42
A cascade connection feeds the output of one system into the input of another. The notes state that LTI systems in cascade can be implemented in either order because convolution is commutative. If two systems have impulse responses h_1[n] and h_2[n], then the equivalent system has impulse response h[n]=h_1[n]*h_2[n]. The diagrams show three equivalent systems: h_1 followed by h_2, h_2 followed by h_1, and one equivalent LTI block with impulse response h_1*h_2. In one example, h_1[n]=\delta[n]+\delta[n-1], h_2[n]=\delta[n]-\delta[n-1], and x[n]=u[n]. Their cascade has equivalent response \delta[n]-\delta[n-2], giving output u[n]-u[n-2], a length-2 pulse starting at n=0. Another example computes w[n]=u[n]*h_1[n] and a longer equivalent impulse response for cascaded systems.

In a cascade connection of two systems, the output of the first

LTI systems have the remarkable property that two LTI

signals-and-systems/causal-and-noncausal.title: Causal and Noncausal Running-Average Filters
signals-and-systems/causal-and-noncausal.content:
Causal and Noncausal Running-Average Filters
Source: Signals and Systems Full Notes: Sinusoids, Spectra, Sampling, Aliasing, and FIR Filters
Locations: Page 28, Page 29
The indexing convention of a running-average filter determines whether it is causal or noncausal. The equation y[n]=\frac{1}{3}(x[n]+x[n+1]+x[n+2]) uses present and future input values relative to index n, so it is noncausal when n represents time. A noncausal filter cannot be implemented in real time because future input samples are unavailable when the output must be computed. The notes describe the running average as a sliding window of three samples that determines which values are used for each output. A causal 3-point running average instead uses the present and past values: y[n]=\frac{1}{3}(x[n]+x[n-1]+x[n-2]). This can also be written as a sum over l from n-2 to n, or as y[n]=\sum_{k=0}^{2}\frac{1}{3}x[n-k]. The same averaging idea is preserved, but the indexing makes the filter realizable in real-time applications.

The notes derive the characteristic equation for a second-order homogeneous constant-coefficient ODE using the system form \vec{X}'=A\vec{X} and the ansatz \vec{X}(t)=e^{rt}\vec{v}. Differentiation gives \vec{X}'=re^{rt}\vec{v}, while the system gives A\vec{X}=Ae^{rt}\vec{v}. Canceling e^{rt} produces the eigenvalue equation A\vec{v}=r\vec{v}. With A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-c/a&-b/a\end{bmatrix}, the determinant condition \det(A-rI)=0 becomes r^2+(b/a)r+c/a=0, or ar^2+br+c=0. The discriminant \Delta=b^2-4ac determines three solution cases. For \Delta>0, two distinct real roots produce y=C_1e^{r_1t}+C_2e^{r_2t}. For \Delta=0, the repeated-root solution is y=C_1e^{rt}+C_2te^{rt}. For complex roots r=\alpha\pm i\beta, the real solution is y=e^{\alpha t}(C_1\cos\beta t+C_2\sin\beta t).

signals-and-systems/closed-loop-characte.title: Closed-Loop Characteristic Equation and Controller Design
signals-and-systems/closed-loop-characte.content:
Closed-Loop Characteristic Equation and Controller Design
Source: Signals and Systems Full Notes: Sinusoids, Spectra, Sampling, Aliasing, and FIR Filters
Locations: Page 107
The notes connect controller design to the poles of the closed-loop system through the characteristic equation. Any physically realizable transfer function can be written as a ratio of polynomials. The plant is written G(s)=b(s)/a(s), and the controller is written D(s)=\ell(s)/d(s). The feedback characteristic equation begins with 1+D(s)G(s)=0. Substituting the polynomial ratios gives 1+b(s)\ell(s)/(d(s)a(s))=0, which is equivalent to a(s)d(s)+b(s)\ell(s)=0. Since the plant polynomials a(s) and b(s) are known, controller design changes \ell(s) and d(s) to shape the roots of this characteristic equation. The notes interpret this as the way controller design solves the stability problem, because closed-loop pole locations determine stability and transient behavior.
Page-grounded details
Page 107
In a bit, we will look at how to design more (and appropriate) controllers
intro better but first, we need the metrics to design said controllers.

Output from the junction is labelled E(s), then enters a block labelled D(s) with “controller” written above it. The output is labelled U(s), then enters a second summing junction. A top downward input labelled W(s) enters this junction with a plus sign. The output then goes into a block labelled G(s), with “plant” written above it. The output arrow is labelled Y(s). From Y(s), a feedback branch goes downward into another summing junction at the lower right. A downward input labelled V(s) enters this lower summing junction; both inputs are marked plus. The output of this lower summing junction runs left along the bottom and up into the negative input of the first summing junction. A realizable controller can be written D(s)=\ell(s)/d(s).
The closed-loop characteristic equation starts from 1+D(s)G(s)=0.
Substitution gives a(s)d(s)+b(s)\ell(s)=0.
The plant polynomials are known, while controller polynomials are design variables.
Changing controller polynomials changes closed-loop roots and therefore stability.

Page 107 defines a classical closed-loop system with controller D(s), plant G(s), reference R(s), plant-input disturbance W(s), and sensor measurement noise V(s). The measured feedback signal is Y+V, so the error is E=R-(Y+V)=R-Y-V. The controller output is U=DE=D(R-Y-V), and the plant output is modeled as Y=G(U+W). Solving the loop gives the output as a superposition of reference, disturbance, and measurement-noise effects: Y(s)=\frac{DG}{1+DG}R+\frac{G}{1+DG}W-\frac{DG}{1+DG}V. The control signal and error are also decomposed into terms driven by R, W, and V. This form shows why the closed-loop transfer function T_{cl}=GD/(1+GD) is only one part of the complete performance description; disturbance and noise paths matter too.

signals-and-systems/complex-numbers-pola.content:
Complex Numbers, Polar Form, and Euler Identity
Source: Signals and Systems Full Notes: Sinusoids, Spectra, Sampling, Aliasing, and FIR Filters
Locations: Page 4, Page 5
Complex numbers are introduced as a foundation for complex exponential signals and phasors. A complex number z\in\mathbb{C} is an ordered pair of real numbers with Cartesian representation z=(x,y) or z=x+jy, where x=\operatorname{Re}(z), y=\operatorname{Im}(z), and j=\sqrt{-1}. In the complex or Argand plane, the real part is the horizontal coordinate and the imaginary part is the vertical coordinate. Because complex numbers can be viewed like vectors in a two-dimensional plane, they can also be represented in polar form as z=re^{j\theta} or phasor notation r\angle\theta, where r=|z| and \theta=\operatorname{Arg}(z). Conversion from polar to Cartesian uses x=r\cos\theta and y=r\sin\theta; conversion from Cartesian to polar uses r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} and an argument calculation. Since ordinary \arctan(y/x) cannot distinguish quadrants, the notes give a piecewise rule for choosing the correct argument. Euler’s identity, e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta, makes polar form algebraically useful.

Conjugate Symmetry and Line Spectra

The notes define the spectrum as a set of frequency-amplitude pairs (f_k,a_k), where a_k is the complex amplitude. For k=0, a_k=A_0; for nonzero sinusoidal components, a_k=\frac{1}{2}A_ke^{j\theta_k}. This allows the signal to be expressed compactly as \sum_{k=-N}^{N}a_ke^{j2\pi f_kt}. A line spectrum plots each frequency component as a vertical line at the appropriate frequency, with length proportional to |a_k|, and labels each spectral line with the value of a_k. The example signal x(t)=10+14\cos(200\pi t+\pi/3)-8\cos(500\pi t+\pi/2) has spectrum lines at 0, \pm100, and \pm200 in the plotted example, with the zero-frequency line labeled 10. For real signals, the negative-frequency complex amplitude is the complex conjugate of the corresponding positive-frequency amplitude; this is called conjugate symmetry. If a spectrum is requested in re^{j\theta} form with r>0, a negative magnitude can be converted by adding a phase of \pi.

signals-and-systems/continuous-time-lti-.content:
Continuous-Time LTI System Properties
Source: Signals and Systems Full Notes: Sinusoids, Spectra, Sampling, Aliasing, and FIR Filters
Locations: Page 62, Page 63
The notes introduce continuous-time LTI systems as single-input single-output systems that transform time functions into other time functions. Engineering is described as the science of transforming signals, where a continuous-time signal is a function of time carrying information and a system is a physical or computational mechanism that manipulates it. Physical systems evolve in time and store energy, so they have memory and are modeled as dynamical systems by differential equations. A continuous-time LTI mapping T sends functions of time to functions of time and satisfies linearity and time invariance. Linearity consists of homogeneity and additivity: scaling the input scales the output, and adding inputs adds outputs. Time invariance means delaying the input by T delays the output by the same amount. Causality means the output depends only on present and past input values, so if u(t)=0 for all t<0, then y(t)=0 for all t<0.

signals-and-systems/continuous-time-sinu.content:
Continuous-Time Sinusoidal Signal Parameters
Source: Signals and Systems Full Notes: Sinusoids, Spectra, Sampling, Aliasing, and FIR Filters
Locations: Page 1
A continuous-time sinusoidal signal is represented by a cosine whose angle is a function of time. The general two-parameter frequency form is x(t)=A\cos(\omega_0t+\phi)=A\cos(2\pi f_0t+\phi), with \omega_0=2\pi f_0. The amplitude A scales the waveform, so because \cos\theta ranges from -1 to +1, the signal ranges from -A to +A. The phase \phi is measured in radians and determines the starting point or horizontal position of the signal within its cycle. The radian frequency \omega_0 has units rad/s when time is in seconds, while the cyclic frequency f_0 has units s^{-1}, hertz, or cycles per second. Sine waves are converted to cosine form because the notes use cosine as the standard sinusoid: A\sin(\omega_0t+\phi)=A\cos(\omega_0t+\pi/2+\phi). The periodicity of cosine is expressed by \cos x=\cos a \Leftrightarrow x=\pm a+2\pi k, k\in\mathbb{Z}.

a) A is called the Amplitude which is a scaling factor that determines how large
the cosine signal will be. Since cos θ oscillates between -1, +1, signal
x(t) oscillates between -A, +A
b) φ is called the phase, in radians which is its starting point or horizontal
position within its cycle.

be in radians which is dimensionless, the quantity ω_0t must likewise be dimensionless
∴ ω_0 must have units of rad/s if t has units of seconds. Similarly

signals-and-systems/differential-equatio.content:
Differential Equation Classification and Solutions
Source: Signals and Systems Full Notes: Sinusoids, Spectra, Sampling, Aliasing, and FIR Filters
Locations: Page 43, Page 44, Page 45
The notes introduce differential equations as equations relating the rate of change of a function to how it changes through space and time. Newton’s second law is used as a familiar example: since acceleration can be written as a=dv/dt or a=d^2u/dt^2, F=ma becomes a differential equation such as F(t,v)=m\,dv/dt or F(t,u,du/dt)=m\,d^2u/dt^2. Differential equations are classified as ordinary when derivatives are with respect to one variable and partial when derivatives involve multiple variables. Their order is the highest derivative appearing. A linear differential equation has the form a_n(t)y^{(n)}(t)+a_{n-1}(t)y^{(n-1)}(t)+\cdots+a_1y'(t)+a_0y(t)=g(t), with no products of y and its derivatives. The notes distinguish general solutions, which contain arbitrary constants and represent a family of curves, from particular solutions, which satisfy initial conditions and select one trajectory.
Page-grounded details
Page 43

Chapter 1 Differential Equations:
1.1. Definitions
A differential equation, in short, is an equation relating the rate
of change of a function, or its derivative, to how it changes through
space and time.
There is one differential equation that everybody knows, that is

signals-and-systems/dirac-delta-distribu.content:
Dirac Delta Distribution
Source: Signals and Systems Full Notes: Sinusoids, Spectra, Sampling, Aliasing, and FIR Filters
Locations: Page 64
The Dirac delta distribution is introduced as the continuous-time impulse, analogous in role to the discrete unit impulse but not an ordinary classical function. The notes visualize it as a rectangle centered at the origin with width \Delta and height 1/\Delta, so its area is always one. As \Delta shrinks toward zero, the rectangle becomes an infinitely narrow and infinitely tall spike while preserving area one. This limiting object is the Dirac delta. It is defined by the integral condition \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(x)\,dx=1. Heuristically, the notes write that \delta(x)=0 for x\neq0 and \delta(x)=\infty for x=0, while emphasizing that it is not an ordinary function. This concept supports the extension of impulse-response and convolution ideas from discrete-time LTI systems to continuous-time LTI systems.

Direction fields visualize the behavior of solutions to a differential equation without solving it explicitly. They show the slope of the solution curve at each point, allowing sketches of solution trajectories and analysis of long-term behavior. The notes connect direction fields to modeling by deriving a falling-object equation under gravity and quadratic air resistance. Taking downward velocity as positive gives gravitational force F_G=mg and air resistance F_A=-\gamma v^2. Newton’s law yields m\,dv/dt=mg-\gamma v^2, or dv/dt=g-(\gamma/m)v^2. The field shows solutions below v=50 increasing, solutions above v=50 decreasing, and all solutions approaching v=50 as t\to\infty.

The discrete convolution sum expresses the output of an FIR or LTI system in terms of the input sequence and impulse response. For an FIR filter, because the coefficients equal the impulse response samples, the output can be written as y[n]=\sum_{k=0}^{M}h[k]x[n-k]. signals-and-systems/discrete-time-aliase.content:
Discrete-Time Aliases and Principal Frequency
Source: Signals and Systems Full Notes: Sinusoids, Spectra, Sampling, Aliasing, and FIR Filters
Locations: Page 18, Page 19
Aliases arise because discrete-time sinusoidal frequencies differing by integer multiples of 2\pi can produce identical sample values. The notes illustrate this with x_1[n]=\cos(0.4\pi n) and x_2[n]=\cos(2.4\pi n). Since x_2[n]=\cos(2\pi n+0.4\pi n)=\cos(0.4\pi n) for integer n, the two formulas are different names for the same sequence. The general alias frequencies of 0.4\pi are \hat{\omega}_\ell=0.4\pi+2\pi\ell, with integer \ell. The principal alias is the unique alias in the interval -\pi<\hat{\omega}\le\pi. A folded alias also occurs because cosine is even: A\cos((2\pi-\hat{\omega})n-\phi)=A\cos(\hat{\omega}n+\phi), so the sign of phase for folded aliases must be opposite to the sign of the principal alias phase. The notes summarize aliases of a sinusoid as \hat{\omega}_0, \hat{\omega}_0+2\pi\ell, and 2\pi\ell-\hat{\omega}_0.

Discrete-Time Linearity and Time Invariance
Source: Signals and Systems Full Notes: Sinusoids, Spectra, Sampling, Aliasing, and FIR Filters

A discrete-time LTI system is defined by two properties: linearity and time invariance. Linearity means superposition holds: if x_1[n] produces y_1[n] and x_2[n] produces y_2[n], then \alpha x_1[n]+\beta x_2[n] produces \alpha y_1[n]+\beta y_2[n]. Time invariance means that delaying the input by n_0 delays the output by the same amount. The notes test time invariance by comparing the output of a delayed input with the delayed version of the original output. The system y[n]=nx[n] is not time invariant because a delayed input gives nx[n-n_0], whereas delaying the original output gives (n-n_0)x[n-n_0]. The system y[n]=(x[n])^2 is not linear because (\alpha x_1[n]+\beta x_2[n])^2 is not equal to \alpha(x_1[n])^2+\beta(x_2[n])^2. These tests establish when convolution-based LTI theory applies.

signals-and-systems/discrete-time-system.title: Discrete-Time Systems and FIR Filters
signals-and-systems/discrete-time-system.content:
Discrete-Time Systems and FIR Filters
Source: Signals and Systems Full Notes: Sinusoids, Spectra, Sampling, Aliasing, and FIR Filters
Locations: Page 26
A discrete-time system transforms an input sequence into an output sequence through a computational process. The notes use the notation x[n]\xrightarrow{T}y[n] to state that an operator T maps the input sequence x to the output sequence y. Since a discrete-time signal is a sequence of values, the operator can be described by a formula for computing each output value from input values. A simple example is y[n]=(x[n])^2, where each output sample is the square of the corresponding input sample. Discrete-time systems operate entirely on discrete-time signals, unlike sampling and reconstruction systems that convert between continuous and discrete time. The notes place such systems inside a broader processing chain where x(t) is sampled by a C/D block, processed by T, and reconstructed by a D/C block. The chapter begins the study of FIR filters, described as finite impulse response filters and as a very important class of discrete-time systems that are part of linear time-invariant systems.

A discrete-time system transforms an input sequence into an output

signals-and-systems/discrete-unit-impuls.title: Discrete Unit Impulse Sequence
signals-and-systems/discrete-unit-impuls.content:
Discrete Unit Impulse Sequence
Source: Signals and Systems Full Notes: Sinusoids, Spectra, Sampling, Aliasing, and FIR Filters
Locations: Page 30, Page 31
The discrete unit impulse sequence, also called the Kronecker delta, is the basic building block for representing discrete-time signals. It is defined to be one at the origin and zero everywhere else. A shifted impulse \delta[n-k] is nonzero only when its argument is zero, so \delta[n-2] has its only nonzero value at n=2. The notes use this fact to show that finite sequences can be decomposed into weighted and shifted impulses. For example, the sequence x[n]=\{2,4,6,4,2\} with the first sample at n=0 can be written as 2\delta[n]+4\delta[n-1]+6\delta[n-2]+4\delta[n-3]+2\delta[n-4]. More generally, any sequence can be represented as a sum over impulse basis elements: x[n]=\sum_k x[k]\delta[n-k]. This representation is foundational because LTI systems are fully characterized by how they respond to shifted impulses.
Page-grounded details

can be expressed as 0 ⇐ k ⇐ N-1. The periodic extension support of the signal then
is an interval of N samples at the origin where the convolution involves
fewer than M-1 nonzero samples as the sliding window of the filter edges
with the input and another M samples at the end where the sliding window
disengages from the input sequence.

The length of the output sequence would be N+M samples where N is the
length of the input signal, M-1 is the filter length and M is the filter order.
